en: Salutations to that Acyuta, who acts with supreme propriety, by whom the eye used for deceiving his enemies was rendered soiled with collyrium. || 1 ||
Having composed the *Kavikaṇikā* and the *Kāvyālaṅkāra*, as well as the *Viveka*— which is dear to the learned— and having also composed the *Yugmaka*, Kṣemendra [has completed these works].

Now he undertakes an investigation of propriety (*aucitya*), which is beautiful and produces aesthetic wonder when savored; which is the very lifeblood of rasa and produces aesthetic wonder when savored; and which constitutes the essence of the life of rasa. (3)
Of what use are ornaments for poetry, or what is the point of falsely enumerating its merits, when its very life—propriety—is not seen even upon reflection? (4)
Ornaments are indeed ornaments, and virtues are always virtues;
however, appropriateness is the enduring life of poetry perfected by rasa. (5)

In poetry, which consists of words and meanings that delight through the mutual assistance of human beings, those abundant ornaments such as simile (*upamā*) and poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) are indeed merely "ornaments" (*alaṅkāra*), like bracelets, earrings, armlets, and necklaces, because they are the cause of external beauty. Furthermore, whatever poetic qualities (*guṇa*) have been enumerated by those expert in its definition are also merely "qualities," like innate virtues such as truthfulness and courage, because they are inherent. However, propriety (*aucitya*), whose definition will be stated later, is the stable and imperishable life-force of poetry; without it, this [poetry] would not exist.

Because even that which is endowed with poetic qualities (guṇa) and ornaments (alaṅkāra) is devoid of life; the meaning is that for poetry—which is established and renowned through *rasa*, such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others—it is like the stable vitality of one who has achieved alchemical mastery over the essences of metals.
He states a further distinction regarding this very point already mentioned:
Adornment consists in the arrangement of parts in their appropriate places;
like you, O Lord, virtues are truly virtues only when they never deviate from propriety.

An ornament becomes capable of adorning when it is placed in a suitable location; otherwise, it does not even deserve the designation "ornament. In the same way, the *guṇas* (excellences) attain the status of being *guṇas* only when they do not deviate from propriety (*aucitya*); otherwise, they are merely non-excellences (*aguṇas*).
As it has been said:
A girdle around the neck, a large pearl necklace on the surface of the hips,

anklets on the hands, or bracelets on the feet— when an enemy has been humbled by one’s majesty, what does not become an object of ridicule? Without propriety (*aucitya*), there is neither beauty in a sentiment nor virtue in a quality.
What is that propriety? He says:
"The teachers declare that 'propriety' (ācita) is indeed that which is appropriate to each individual."
And the state of that which is insentient is what they call propriety (aucitya). || 7 ||
That which is indeed appropriate for something is called "fitting" (*ucita*); they describe its state as "propriety" (*aucitya*).
Now, in order to demonstrate the preeminent status of propriety—which serves as the very life-force of the body of all poetry—he says:
"In the word, in the sentence, in the meaning of the composition, in the quality (*guṇa*), in the ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)."
In the case of an action, an agent, a verbal suffix, a number, and a qualifier. (8)
In the case of a prefix, a particle, time, place, family, a vow, reality, existence, and non-grasping. || 9 ||

They say that appropriateness (*aucitya*)—pervasive and the very lifeblood—is present in inspiration, in the state [of the speaker], in the fourfold division, in the name, in the benediction, and in the constituent parts of poetry. (10)

In these locations, beginning with the words and so forth, as well as in the vital points (*marmas*) of poetry, propriety (*aucitya*), which pervades the entire body of the work, manifests clearly as something vividly apparent.
To show examples of these in their proper order, he says:

"An eloquent composition, bearing its *tilaka* (mark), shines with a single appropriate word, just as a dark-complexioned woman with a moon-like face shines when she has applied musk and sandalwood paste. (11)
A single well-composed word, appearing like a decorative mark (*tilaka*), brings about a state of exquisite beauty through its excellence when it possesses a fittingly superior quality;
just as the families of enemies, submerged in the battle thick with the edge of your sword, are overwhelmed by fragrance.
O King, having long ago heard the words of bards repeatedly saying, "The Lord is here," the innocent queen of the Gurjara king, bewildered by her hope for water in the wilderness,
keeps casting her eyes again and again upon her husband’s sword.

Here, the elegant expression (*sūkti*), graced by the word "innocent" (*mugdha*) which evokes aesthetic charm through propriety, spreads a unique grace (*vicchitti*) that serves as the ornament of the entire lineage of poets—just as an autumn moon with a dark mole on its face, or a white forehead-mark with a dark tilaka. It is not, however, like that of Dharmakīrti: *“The world is full of suffering, and there is no happiness anywhere; O friend, this is the truth, for what else could it be?”* In this case, the word “friend” (*sakhe*) is merely a vocative particle (*nipāta*) used to address someone; it does not possess the power to produce the intended meaning. Therefore, it is not a true poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*). Furthermore, the word “world” (*jagat*) is a common noun (*nāman*), and the word “suffering” (*duḥkha*) is an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*); thus, they do not constitute a *samāsokti*. Nor is it a *parikara*, because the adjectives do not serve to characterize the subject through their own specific qualities. Nor is it a *śleṣa*, because the words are not intended to convey a double meaning. Nor is it a *vyatireka*, because there is no comparison between the two things. Nor is it a *pratīpa*, because the object of comparison is not being denied. Nor is it a *tulyayogitā*, because the various actions are not being performed by multiple subjects simultaneously. Nor is it a *dīpaka*, because the single action is not illuminating multiple subjects. Nor is it a *yathāsaṃkhya*, because the sequence of the objects does not correspond to the sequence of the verbs. Nor is it a *preyas*, because the excellence of the object is not being expressed. Nor is it a *rasavat*, because the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) is not being manifested. Nor is it a *ūrjasvin*, because there is no manifestation of power. Nor is it a *samāhita*, because there is no subordination of one thing to another. Nor is it a *bhāvika*, because there is no vivid representation of past or future events. Nor is it a *udātta*, because there is no description of greatness. Nor is it a *apahnuti*, because there is no concealment of one thing by another. Nor is it a *utprekṣā*, because there is no imaginative conceit. Nor is it a *atiśayokti*, because there is no exaggeration. Nor is it a *svabhāvokti*, because there is no description of the inherent nature of things. Nor is it a *vibhāvanā*, because the effect is not produced despite the absence of its cause. Nor is it a *viśeṣokti*, because the non-occurrence of the effect despite the presence of the cause is not described. Nor is it a *hetu*, because the cause is not explicitly stated. Nor is it a *kāvyaliṅga*, because there is no logical connection between the cause and the effect. Nor is it a *arthāntaranyāsa*, because there is no generalization or particularization. Nor is it a *prativastūpamā*, because there is no similarity between two distinct things. Nor is it a *dṛṣṭānta*, because there is no illustration. Nor is it a *nidarśanā*, because there is no depiction of a relationship. Nor is it a *vyājastuti*, because there is no praise or censure under the guise of something else. Nor is it a *ākṣepa*, because there is no denial of a statement. Nor is it a *virodha*, because there is no apparent contradiction. Nor is it a *samāsokti*, because the meaning is not conveyed through a compound. Nor is it a *parikara*, because the adjectives do not characterize the subject. Nor is it a *śliṣṭa-rūpaka*, because there is no metaphorical identification. Nor is it a *sahokti*, because the simultaneous occurrence of two things is not described. Nor is it a *vinokti*, because there is no description of something as being without another. Nor is it a *anyonyam*, because there is no mutual relation. Nor is it a *parivṛtti*, because there is no exchange
The expenditure of salt and wealth was not reckoned, great hardships were voluntarily endured, and the fever of anxiety was inflicted upon people living in freedom for the sake of happiness;
yet even this wretched woman, though possessing a lover equal to herself, has been destroyed by her own feelings.
What purpose was placed in the mind by the Creator while fashioning the body for this slender maiden?

In this context, the word *tanvyāḥ* ("of the slender one") has been composed out of a mere addiction to verbal alliteration (*śabdānuprāsa*) and does not manifest even a grain of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) appropriate to the sense. The word *sundaryāḥ* ("of the beautiful one") would be more suitable here, or other words that suggest unsurpassed beauty and loveliness. However, the word *tanvī* produces a sense of inappropriateness (*anucitārthatva*) when applied to a woman distressed by separation.
As in Śrī Harṣa’s [verse]:
"Faded on both sides from contact with her full breasts and hips, yet not having reached the greenness of the interior due to the crushing of the body,
this [garland] has its arrangement disordered by the tossing and twisting of her creeper-like arms."
The bed of lotus leaves speaks of the torment of one with emaciated limbs.
In this context, the word "emaciated limbs," which indicates Sāgarikā’s state of separation, nourishes the highest degree of propriety. || 11 ||
To demonstrate the propriety inherent in speech, he says:
"Speech composed with propriety is always esteemed by the virtuous, like sovereignty exalted by generosity or sacred learning radiant with good character. (12)
A sentence composed with propriety is most highly esteemed by those who possess discernment regarding poetry;
as in this pair of verses (*yugmaka*) of mine from the *Vinayavallī*:

"The god Vijaya is compassionate and self-conquered; the two Yamas are worthy of honor for their mental restraint"—saying this, he stroked his own arm, which was like the staff of Death raised against Kīcaka.

That enemy of Kirmīra and Jaṭāsura, who was the instructor in subduing the prowess of Kubera, the beloved of Hiḍimbā, and the Yama who brought about the final reckoning for the Kurus—was he seen as milk? Or was he the one who taught the restraint of Kubera’s valor? Indeed, he was the one who made the calculation of the boundary lines for the beautiful women of the Kurus.

Here, through words such as *bhauma* (the son of Bhūmi), *bhīmacarita* (of terrifying deeds), *ucitakocaka* (fittingly dark), *kālikakāladaṇḍa* (the black staff of Time), and *hiḍimbādayitā* (the lover of Hiḍimbā), the meaning of the sentence— which corresponds to the essential nature of the *raudra* (furious) sentiment— shines forth as if it were alive.
Alternatively,

[the moon] is the beloved of the wives of the stars, who is the kinsman of kings, the preceptor for the initiation into the amorous activities of many monarchs, and one well-acquainted with the comparison to the face of the fair-limbed Gaurī.
O beautiful one, behold here this moon, the crest-jewel of Śiva, possessing a brilliance as white as the teeth of a young Southern maiden freshly ground.

Here too, the sentence-meaning, brought about by words that are internal to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and which kindle the god of love (*anaṅga*), has attained an extreme degree of desirability through the power of universal propriety and the force of a suitable meaning;
yet it is not as in this very [other example].
He was the vast stalk of the great lotus of valor, the bridge over the ocean of enemies, the ever-present sandalwood tree for those who wielded the sword,
the playground of Fortune, the lofty peak of the elephant of victory, and the supreme pride of the God of Love for beautiful-eyed women.
May the world rejoice, nestled upon the arm of the illustrious Duryodhana, which is intent on valor.

Here, the meaning of the sentence is understood as being composed with a sense of mockery, through the inappropriate comparison of the pillar-like arm of that exceedingly fierce and pre-eminent hero to a lotus stalk. 12.
In order to demonstrate the propriety of the meaning of the *prabandha* (the literary composition), he says:
"The meaning of the *prabandha* is revealed by way of its appropriate specific meaning, just as a virtuous person is revealed by his prosperity consisting of the power of his qualities. (13)

A great poem attains a state of wondrous beauty through specific appropriate meanings that act as a shower of nectar, nourishing the entire subject matter of the composition, and which are conceived by the excellence of unfading eloquence;
as, for example, in the works of Kālidāsa.
Born in the lineage of the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds that pervade the world,

I know you to be the primordial spirit (prakṛtipuruṣa) of Indra, able to assume any form at will. Therefore, though my kinsmen are far away, I have come here as a suppliant, driven by the power of destiny.
A request made to one of superior virtue is better than one to an incapable person, for it is fulfilled according to one's desire.

In this context, by introducing the fact that the cloud—though insentient—is descended from the renowned lineage of the Puṣkarāvartaka rain-clouds and possesses the nature of a ministerial servant, in order to establish its fitness for the role of a messenger through the superimposition of sentience, the unsurpassed propriety (*aucitya*) of the entire composition, which is rendered most beautiful by its imagined plot, is illuminated.
Or as in the case of Bhavabhūti’s [verse]: "Is this a horse, or is it this banner, or perhaps a proclamation of heroism?"
Of the sole hero of the seven worlds, the enemy of the ten Kāṇva clans.
Latra: Oh, what scorching words! O, O! Is the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas that it is proclaimed thus? Ah! Do weapons even quiver?

This bow—its fierce-tipped teeth encircled by the tongue of the string, emitting a deep *gharghara* roar like the belching of a cloud—mocks the gaping mouth of Death as he laughs, intent upon devouring his prey. It stands with its formidable form trembling.

In this matter, by departing from the narrative of the *Rāmāyaṇa*, a new poetic imagination presents the ground for the excellence of valor—a natural prowess following the footsteps of Rāma’s own son—namely, an invulnerability to the touch of another's majesty; this bestows upon the composition a grace of propriety that is rich in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
For Rāvaṇa [could not even approach] the hand of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), which had remained for a thousand autumns delighted by its forceful grasping of Pārvatī’s hair.
May that bow appear—the price for the purchase of the Maithilī, which caused the limbs of the gods to quiver with the mere sight of its tip.
"Let Janaka appear together with Sītā, who was born from the earth.

Here, by Janaka’s statement "let [he] appear together with Sītā," it appears as if the king intends to bestow his daughter upon a man-eater (*piśitāśana*). Now, we do not know how this can be; for how can one whose limbs are as tender as a flower be bestowed upon a cannibal? This well-known violation of propriety (*anaucitya*) and reversal of the established course of action (*vṛttavaiparītya*) brings about a profound discord in the heart.
Or as Kālidāsa [wrote]: "At that moment, Hara, his eyes stolen by the rows of nail-marks at the base of her thighs,
prevented his beloved from adjusting her loosened garment."

In this description of the amorous union with Ambikā, the fact that the eyes of the three-eyed Lord—the teacher of the three worlds—were captivated by her thighs, which were adorned with a row of hair characteristic of modest noble women (rather than commoners), serves to nourish the very theme of the composition: namely, the supreme *anaucitya* (inappropriateness). || 13 ||
To demonstrate the accumulation of qualities, he says:
In a beautiful poem, a quality that is appropriate to the subject at hand is itself beautiful and possesses charm;
arising at the occasion of enjoyment, it causes a flow of bliss like a mouse [squeaking]. (14)

In poetry, the quality (*guṇa*)— characterized by *ojas*, *prasāda*, *mādhurya*, *saukumārya*, and so forth— becomes manifest through the appropriateness of the subject matter; having attained a state of auspiciousness, it distills a mass of joy for the connoisseurs, just as the moon does.

In this passage, Kādambarī’s description of the agony of separation—her fortitude shattered by the weight of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation)—spreads a state of supreme endearment that gladdens the heart through her pleasant speech, owing to her possession of qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and delicacy (*saukumārya*), much like the full moon.
For instance: "In the battles of Candraka, where fortune wavers, there is no promise for me."
Fate ordains both victory and defeat;
this indeed has always been my vow when I have gone to battle: that my enemies shall not behold the rear of my horses.

In this regard, the speech of a great warrior, though appropriate in its meaning, does not shine—being devoid of the life-force of brilliance due to its lack of poetic quality, like the flame of a lamp in a pauper’s house that grows dim; it is as if the conduct of a kṣatriya were untouched by vigor.
Or, for example, as in the case of Rājaśekhara:
The fever of love for her cannot be tested by the touch of palms, as even a gentle person, fearing the burning heat, would withdraw his hand from water boiling on a stove; yet,
when that [fever] has rendered the medicinal applications of sandalwood and camphor powerless, it crackles like lightning.
All these jewels of the pearl necklaces burst open like parched grain.

In this context, discarding the sweetness appropriate to the state of love-stricken women distressed by separation, the statement that "the parched grains burst with a crackling sound" is harsh; though it flashes with the power of *ojas* (vigorous energy), this well-spoken verse—like a graceful woman who speaks roughly—is charmingly beautiful yet harsh, and instantly instills a sense of impropriety in the mind. || 14 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of ornamentation, he says:
"Furthermore, speech endowed with propriety shines by means of an ornament, just as a fawn-eyed woman shines with a necklace resting upon her full breasts. (15)
A well-spoken verse shines through the use of figures of speech such as simile (*upamā*) or poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), which accord with the propriety of the subject at hand,
just as a beautiful string of pearls shines while kissing the high breasts of a loving woman.
For example, that of Śrī Harṣa:
Having ceased all talk of war,
dwelling with delight in the hearts of the people, he is truly Priyavasantaka himself, now filled with longing to witness his own great festival.
The Lord of Vatsa approaches, as formidable as the flower-bowed god of love.

In this passage, the comparison of the Lord of Vatsa to the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāmadeva) reveals, through its propriety, an indescribable heart-stirring quality of exquisite beauty suited to the occasion of the erotic sentiment;
it is not, however, as in the case of Candraka’s verse:
"A swing was fashioned upon the tree-top by the entrails flung up by birds..."
The jackal, satisfied with her meal, sleeps like a woman exhausted by lovemaking;
the thirsty jackal licks the blood-stained sword many times;
and the serpent, seeking a hole, enters the hollow of the slain elephant's trunk.

In this case, the comparison of a female jackal— standing in an improper place, satiated with human flesh, and howling— to the beauty of a woman exhausted at the end of amorous play, reveals nothing but a complete perversion [of the intended meaning].
Or, for example, as in the verse of Mālava-rudra:

The taste of anger in those whose beards are newly grown; the frosty wind, harsh from contact with the dry dung-fires; the sun’s light now dull as its power has faded; and the moon bears the likeness of the face of a woman separated from her lover. Such is the condition of the command of one whose wealth has vanished.

Here, the similarity between the anger of a delicate young woman and a fire of dried cow-dung—though beautiful because it resonates with the heart due to the sweetness of the cold season—is made to convey, by its very impropriety, a sudden contraction of the mind as if it were a physical shrinking.
Or, for example, as in Rājaśekhara’s verse:
"The moon is the funeral pyre-circle for the bodiless Love-god whose body was consumed by fire..."
The moon there assumes the appearance of soiled charcoal;
for this ash, mixed with bits of camphor broken by the light, spreads in every direction, scattered by the winds.

In this case as well, the fact that the moon—beautiful with its flowing stream of nectar and bliss—is the fuel for the circle of funeral pyres (the *citācakra*) brings about a harshness to the ear like a crow's cawing, due to its impropriety. However, whatever meaning resonates with the heart, if it is entirely free from even a trace of the touch of impropriety, then it nourishes the splendor of the poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) to the highest degree. For example, [the verse describing] a traveler, unheeded by the cold, sinking into an ocean of thoughts regarding beans and lentils: *...māṣaśimivacyintārṇave majjataḥ...* [etc. [The full verse: "O traveler, you who are unheeded by the cold, why do you not abandon this body which is but a vessel of suffering? Why do you not abandon this life which is but a source of misery? Why do you not abandon this world which is but a mass of delusion? Why do you not abandon this mind which is but a nest of desires? Alas, traveler, you are sinking in an ocean of thoughts of beans and lentils; why do you not wake up? In this instance, the intended meaning—which is the awakening of the traveler—is entirely free from any touch of impropriety, and thus it greatly enhances the beauty of the poetic ornament. This is because the intended meaning here is the awakening of the traveler, and since that awakening is not inconsistent with the context, it does not produce any harshness to the ear. Therefore, the impropriety is not perceived. On the other hand, in the previous example, the intended meaning was the burning of the moon, and since that burning is inconsistent with the context, it produces a harshness to the ear. Thus, the impropriety is clearly perceived there. Consequently, the former is more beautiful than the latter. Therefore, the definition of impropriety is: "that which, while being the intended meaning, is inconsistent with the context. This is established. Furthermore, this impropriety is divided into two types: that pertaining to the speaker and that pertaining to the expressed object. Of these, the former is illustrated by the following: "A woman whose husband has gone abroad, having heard of his death, yet seeing him alive, speaks thus to her female friend: *...sā bālā virahāturāpi sahate dīnaṃ na dainyaṃ punaḥ...* [etc. "In this case, the intended meaning is the concealment of her own grief by the woman whose husband has gone abroad; however, that concealment is inconsistent with the context, and thus it produces a harshness to the ear. For me, whose fires have been extinguished, whose syllables are faltering, and whose throat is parched by hunger,
sleep has gone far away as if insulted by my beloved;
yet the night does not diminish, like wealth bestowed upon a worthy recipient.
In this case, by avoiding any touch of impropriety, only the beauty that resonates with the heart provides the most delicious delight. || 15 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of aesthetic flavor (rasaucitya), he says:
"The aesthetic flavor, beautiful through its propriety, pervading all that remains, causes the mind to sprout like the month of Madhu [the spring] does for the Aśoka tree. (16)

The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), characterized by the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other sentiments, when radiant through propriety (*aucitya*), pervades the hearts of all people; like the spring season, it causes the mind to bud forth with longing, as in the verse of Śrī Harṣa:
"Her passion (*utkalikā*) is intense, her luster is pale-white, and in an instant she begins to yawn, spreading her own exhaustion through incessant, deep sighs."
Today, beholding this garden creeper, which like another woman is possessed of the *madana* flower, I shall cause the face of the Queen to take on a hue as crimson as anger.

In this passage, the brilliance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), which takes the form of jealousy and separation as it is observed in Vāsavadattā, is rendered exceedingly charming and wondrous through the superimposition of the state of separation upon the *nabhamālikā* creeper, owing to its resemblance to a graceful woman.
Or, for example, as in Kālidāsa’s verse:
"The *palāśa* flowers, curved like the young moon and intensely red, shone because they lacked the state of blossoming."
They were like fresh nail-marks upon the forest grounds, left by Spring as he embraced them.

Here, in the context of the Supreme Lord’s longing for Pārvatī—a state of love (*śṛṅgāra*) that will be described—the description of spring as the first of the excitant factors (*uddīpanavibhāva*) achieves the highest degree of propriety and beauty by superimposing the nature of a lover upon it; thus, the forest grounds, which are like young women, are imagined to bear nail-marks suitable for a fresh union in the form of the curved, red buds of the *palāśa* tree. This is not, however, as in the following example: [The verse: "O friend, the *palāśa* tree, with its red flowers, appears to have been wounded by the nails of the Spring-Lord, who, having stolen the pride of the *campaka*, has now embraced the *mālatī*. In this case, the superimposition of the lover's nature is not appropriate. Why? Because the *palāśa* is not a woman, nor is the spring a man; rather, they are simply things. Furthermore, since the *palāśa* is not a woman, it cannot be said that the *mālatī* was stolen from her; and since the spring is not a man, it cannot be said that he stole the pride of the *campaka*. Therefore, because the metaphorical attribution (*adhyāropa*) is improper, the figure of speech is merely a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), and it does not attain the excellence of the *śṛṅgāra* rasa. When its color was at its peak, the *karṇikāra* flower pained the heart with its lack of fragrance;
for generally, the Creator’s disposition is averse to the complete assembly of all virtues in a single thing.

In this instance, by the mere description of the *karṇikāra* flower—which contains within it the suggestion of the Creator (Brahmā) and is thus irrelevant to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) at hand—nothing has been stated that is appropriate as an excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) for that sentiment.
As for the comic sentiment (*hāsya-rasa*), an example from my own poem titled *Lāvaṇyavatī*:
"Out of fear of contact with wine, why do you not kiss her face? Why do you hide your nose?"
"Listen, listen! You are practicing a harsh austerity; you are dull-witted if you have no courtesan!
Having spoken thus, Vāsantī, her eyes rolling with intoxication, pours liquor upon the bakula tree—Mālatī—who is like the god of love hidden therein.

In this context, the pouring of wine by the Vedic goddess Śarvilāsinī— intended to restore the sapidity of the *kabaka* tree (which had withered like a Vedic scholar, Atri’s son, who remained hidden out of fear of contact with the impure *sīdhu* liquor)— attains a sense of aesthetic propriety (*sacamatkāra-saucitya*) through the touch of the semblance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa-ābhāsa*), which acts as a secondary element, just as the juice of the mango imparts a delightful flavor to excellent wine.

Or, for example, as in my *Lāvaṇyavatī*: "On the very path, a Kerala woman, her foot pierced by a ketaka thorn, hissing with pleasure, was asked by a libertine, 'Oh, do it again and again, so beautifully! and she smiled.
I think that the beloved, momentarily abashed by the gaze of the rogue, spreads a veil over her face with the cloth of moonlight reflected in the mirror.

Here too, through the propriety of the speech and jesting of a crafty libertine, the *hāsya-rasa* (the comic sentiment), permeated by a semblance (*ābhāsa*) of the *śṛṅgāra-rasa* (the erotic sentiment), attains a supreme and wondrous state of full development.
It is not, however, as in the case of Śyāmalaka,
who, intent on kissing her, [let] a tooth fallen from his own mouth [fall] upon hers.
Having brought it to the root of his tongue and made the sound "khāḍ," he spat it out.

In this case, because the sentiment of humor (*hāsyarasa*), being permeated by the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsarasa*)—like a flower-crest smeared with garlic—is not loathsome, the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) of that which was unintended is eclipsed by its extreme impropriety. In the act of kissing an old woman, the saliva reaching the root of the tongue, falling from the teeth, and rolling in the throat constitutes primarily the sentiment of disgust itself, and not the sentiment of humor.
An example of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) is found in my *Munimatamīmāṃsā*.
When Abhimanyu was slain, Subhadrā, crying out "Alas, my child! Alas, my little son! with a voice that made the stones weep, lamented before the son of Pṛthā;
at which even the army horses stood motionless and slow, shedding tears like young blades of grass and turning their ears back toward their drooping flanks.

Here, Subhadrā’s lamentation—which, being appropriate to the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) known as grief produced by the recent separation from her most beloved son, causes even stones to melt at heart—is reflected not only in Arjuna’s mind, but has reached its highest intensity; furthermore, it has even entered the hearts of the animals, the horses, which manifest the awakening of the intense rasa of compassion through such *anubhāvas* as shedding tears, dropping mouthfuls of grass, and standing motionless and slow. It conveys something truly indescribable.
Alas, O mountain for the lineage of the waves of the erotic sentiment! Alas, O crest-jewel of kings!
Alas, O treasury of the nectar of benevolence! Woe, woe, O ocean of wit!
Alas, O lover of the young women of Deva-Ujjayinī, you who are like a second Kandarpa!
Alas, O noble kinsman, alas, O moon of the arts! Where are you? Look upon us!

In this instance, in the verse beginning with "hasasi" (*ahasasi*), grief is merely perceived through words that invoke the virtues of the departed king during his absence; however, no aesthetic transformation (*rasīkaraṇa*) of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) known as grief has been achieved at all through the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
As for the Furious sentiment (*raudra*), an example from Bhartṛnārāyaṇa is as follows:
Whosoever among the Pāṇḍava armies bears a weapon with pride swelling in his own arms;
whosoever belongs to the Pāñcāla clan, whether a child, of advanced age, or even lying in the womb;
whosoever acts as a witness to those deeds and moves against me in battle, and whosoever stands in opposition—[all these shall fall].
Blinded by wrath, I myself am the destroyer of that very person who is himself the ender of the worlds.

Here, the Furious Sentiment (*raudra-rasa*), whose dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is cruel anger, is appropriate; it causes Aśvatthāman’s steadfastness—which has been weakened by the stupor of a painful affliction caused by the uneven poison of indignation following his grief over the slaughter of Droṇa—to collapse as he mounts the resolve for the act of slaughtering even those in the womb, children, and the elderly with his sword. It is not, however, as in the verse of Pravarasena: "When the mass of sparks from the fire of his sword’s luster flashed, dripping with the blood of Danu’s son..."
Fleeing in terror, their garments disarrayed and the ornaments on their breasts fallen away, they were like the great fortune of the Asuras.
When the mass of light from his fingernails, stained with the blood of the lord of the Danujas, shone forth,
the Fortune of the great Asuras fled in agitation, her breast-cloth slipping away.
Thus ends the shadow.

In this instance, because it is devoid of words expressive of anger, there is not even a glimpse of the *raudra-rasa* (the Furious sentiment), which is the primary sentiment appropriate to the subject at hand, due to its mixture with the *bhayānaka-rasa* (the Terrible sentiment). This is evident from the description: "As the mass of light from the nails of that Nṛsiṃha, fixed in the blood of the Lord of the Danujas, shone forth, the Fortune of the Asuras fled away in confusion, her breast-cloth slipping off. Here, by the description of the Daitya-Śrī fleeing in agitation upon contact with the *bībhatsa-rasa* (the Disgusting sentiment) through the phrase "fixed in blood," the *raudra-rasa* is obscured. An example of the *vīra-rasa* (the Heroic sentiment) is found in my own *Nītilatā*:
Having briefly restrained the destructive sharpness appropriate for a Kṣatriya in Bhārgava Muni— who had propitiated Śiva through his valor yet had gone astray in taking up weapons—
he [restrained him] with a frown as crooked as a bow drawn back to the ear.
By which there is established a state consisting of tranquility, which prohibits what is unjust, and is rooted in Brahman.

In this context, when the sage Bhārgava—who was being pointed out from afar by Śuka and Sāraṇa before Rāvaṇa with the words "This is that Rāma"—was about to deviate from the path of taking up arms due to the influence of a majestic splendor inferred from his calm, profound, and steadfast composure, he displayed a frown that broke the form of his sovereignty while instructing him in conduct appropriate to his own lineage; however, this was not natural, for a change of expression arises from the anger of a hero.
Indeed, the state of a hero is serene, sweet, and firm.
What has been stated here is appropriate; for by means of the defeat of Bhārgava, the excellence of the principal hero is established.
Or as in the case of Rājaśekhara:
"In the midst of women, having lost consciousness due to the blow of the heavy mace wielded with ease..."
You have become instantly liable to execution by that King Arjuna, as helpless as a sacrificial animal;

and even he, the son of Jamadagni—who was the slayer of all those arms belonging to the enemies of all kings—having been utterly defeated by him, was spared because he was a brahmin; thus, this Rāma is merely an ascetic.

Here, the majesty of the principal hero is raised to the highest pinnacle through a sequence of ascending steps consisting of the relative superiority of Rāvaṇa, Kārtavīrya, and Jāmadagnya. It is not, however, as in Bhavabhūti’s [Uttararāmacarita]: "Let those elders whose conduct is beyond reproach remain; let me proceed..."

For even in the subduing of a woman, those of great renown possess unimpaired fame in this world; indeed, people are well aware of those three backward steps taken in the battle with Khara, or rather, the skill displayed in the subduing of Indra’s son.

In this context, the poet has brought about the destruction of Kumāra Lava—the son of Rāma, who is not the primary hero, yet who cannot endure the excellence of another’s prowess—by his own words, for the purpose of inflaming the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*). This is improper, as he describes the destruction of the heroic sentiment residing in the principal hero (Rāma)—which constitutes the very life-blood of the entire composition—through the depiction of [Lava's] subduing of Tāḍakā, his departure from the battlefield, and his slaughter of Bālin while engaged in combat. An example of this in the *bhayānaka* (terrifying) sentiment is found in Śrī Harṣa’s [work]:
Dragging down a golden chain that remains after being partially severed from its trunk, this elephant—
its circle of tinkling bells jingling as it moves with playful steps— having traversed the gates,
now enters the king’s palace from the stable.
Moreover,
this dwarf enters out of fear into the inner chamber of the bodice, which has been left unprotected by the eunuchs due to the absence of the crowd of men;
meanwhile, the Kirātas dwelling on the outskirts have defiled his own name with a touch that is truly unworthy of it.
The hunchbacked women walk very slowly and lowly, fearing that their eyes might be noticed by others.

Here, through the depiction of the appropriate gestures and emotional expressions of the women of the inner apartments— such as the elderly, dwarfs, Kirātas, and hunchbacks— who are utterly bewildered by the fear of fleeing amidst the monkeys due to the terror instilled by the sharp fangs and claws [of Rāvaṇa], and who are distressed by the loss of their fortitude because they lack the capacity for manly valor, there shines forth a beautiful propriety that accords with the *bhayānaka* (terrific) sentiment.
This is not like the description of Prince Muktāpīḍa,
who was reared in childhood on handfuls of the tips of wild rice stalks.

Having seen that bull-elephant— who had drunk the remnants of the oblation from the surface of a lotus leaf, and whose cheeks were trembling with the swarm of bees sluggish from intoxication— the ascetic, standing at a distance, looked upon him again and again with both joy and fear.

In this case, because there is no description of the elephant’s striking or distorted movements, and because the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is devoid of its attendant fear-expressions (*anubhāva*) and is merely mentioned by name, there is no perceived excellence of propriety (*aucitya*), as the agitation appropriate to the *bhayānaka* (fearful) rasa is absent.
As for the *bībhatsa* (disgusting), it is as found in my *Munimatamīmāṃsā*:
What is the use of ornaments, fine garments, perfumes, and sandalwood paste for this body, which is the certain abode of all misfortune and a collection of loathsome things—
a body whose interior is filled with excrement, feces, swarms of worms, hair, and a string of entrails?
Even dogs turn their faces away at the very end of the day when it becomes moist with excrement.

Here, through the description of the most loathsome entrails and other internal organs located in the body—appropriate to the transitory emotion (sthāyibhāva) of disgust (jugupsā) colored by the latent impression (vāsanā) of world-weariness (vairāgya)—a supreme nourishment is established that produces a distaste for the conceit of a substantial body.
It is not, however, as in the case of Candaka.
Emaciated, one-eyed, lame, deprived of ears, and lacking a tail; wasted by hunger, parched, his throat tormented by the fragments of skulls from beggars;
his body covered with festering, putrid wounds swarming with worms.
A dog follows a bitch, and this god of love intoxicates even him.

In this case, what is gained by these excessive and persistent descriptions of loathsomeness for a dog—one who delights in chewing impurities, whose body is built up by doubt and disgust, and whose source of birth is inherently repulsive? It is precisely through these qualities pertaining to man that one brings about a supreme reverence characterized by revulsion.
As in the marvelous [sentiment], for example, in the case of Candaka:
"Now, while Kṛṣṇa has gone to his mother's side to play, he has eaten earth at his own will."

"O Kṛṣṇa, is it true? Who said 'the club-wielder'? Open your mouth wide, you who see what is false!"—when his mouth was thus opened, the Mother of the World beheld the entire universe within it; may that Keśava protect you all.

In this case, there is a most appropriate excellence of wonder arising from the child—who, terrified by his mother as she prepares to rebuke him for eating clay (which was marked by the color of a pale limb, hand, and eye)—opens his mouth wide to reveal the entire universe within; and from the mother’s own state of being overwhelmed with maternal affection due to her ignorance of its power.
It is not, however, as in my *Munitomīmāṃsā*: [The verse from the Munitomīmāṃsā follows here.]
He is an unfathomable ocean of all wonders; even more wonderful than that is that the Sage knows it all.
But this is a supreme marvel: that he, though born from a small jar, is able to discern the path of your own wonders—who indeed is capable of measuring it?

Here, by the power of another lord of rivers, through the sage’s drinking of a single handful [of its water], and through the sage born from a small jar, this wondrous expansion of the world—though it had ascended to a state of incomparable astonishment as it was successively traversed—was suddenly cast down, as if by the force of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration), thinking, "This path of such various marvels of the world is boundless; what is there to wonder at? It vanished just as in my *Caturvargasangraha*: "When [the mind] is stilled..."

In wealth there is the fear of disease; in pleasure, the fear of decay; in riches, the fear of fire, kings, and thieves; in service, the fear of a master; in virtue, the fear of the wicked; in one's lineage, the fear of a bad wife;
in honor, the fear of humiliation; in victory, the fear of enemies; and in the body, the fear of Death.
Alas! Everything that is called "fear" would become "fearlessness"; indeed, only dispassion is fearlessness.

In this context, having established that the enjoyments, pleasures, wealth, and so forth desired by all people are to be abandoned because they consist of fear, the author presents dispassion (*vairāgya*) alone as the means for pacifying all fears and exertions, and thus demonstrates that it is most appropriate for one to enter the unimpeded path of the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*).
As it is said in my own *Munimatamīmāṃsā*:
Whether it be a bed of flowers or a stone, a beloved palace or a forest; whether it be soft-to-the-touch silk or even the bark of a tree;
whether it be savory food or mere boiled pulse, or wealth or even blades of grass—[all these are equal].
For among the great-souled ones, there is indeed equality in the inexhaustibility of drinking the nectar of the bliss of tranquility.

In this regard, it has been stated that which is appropriate for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukti*): for the great ones, whose minds are reeling with eternal bliss born from drinking the nectar of supreme happiness—this happiness being intensified by the universal equanimity produced by resting in the essential reality of non-dual manifestation, which is free from the bed of all conceptual constructions—their attitude toward the pleasant and unpleasant, or toward pleasure and pain, is the same.
It is not, however, as in the case of the illustrious King Utpala, who said:
"Whether it be a snake or a necklace, whether it be a powerful enemy or a friend..."
Whether upon a jewel or a clod of earth, on a bed of flowers or a stone slab, on grass or among women, my days pass with an equal eye as I utter "Śiva, Śiva, Śiva" in some sacred forest.

In this context, while describing that state appropriate for one liberated while living—which is characterized by the subsiding of attachment and aversion toward the pleasant and unpleasant, which is capable of attaining liberation, and which consists of universal equanimity in the form of viewing friend and foe as equal like a snake-catcher—what was stated in a certain sacred forest appears inappropriate, as it conveys a dualistic view and is contrary to the cultivation of non-duality.

For one whose knot of pride regarding duality has dissolved through the attainment of universal equanimity that has reached its peak, who perceives everything everywhere as consisting of Śiva, and who—being satisfied by the realization of the stainless Self—is equal-minded toward both a penance grove and a heap of refuse in a city, even the speech of a merchant or the like is merely an improper utterance for him.

Just as sweet, bitter, and other tastes, when skillfully combined, attain a variety of exquisite flavors, so too do the erotic and other sentiments [attain their fullness] when combined with one another. (17)
One should ensure the preservation of propriety through their mutual conjunction; for to whom is a mixture of sentiments (rasasaṅkara) pleasing when it is touched by impropriety? (18)

Just as pungent, sweet, sour, salty, and other tastes, when combined by a skilled cook in dishes such as *vesavāra* and drinks, attain a variety of flavors, so too do the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and other sentiments when they are not mutually contradictory. Therefore, one should guard the propriety (*aucitya*), which is the very life-blood of their mutual relationship as primary and subordinate elements. The meaning is that the union of sentiments, when touched by the dust of impropriety, is not desired by anyone. Regarding the propriety of the blending of sentiments, an example of the relationship between the primary and subordinate elements of *śānta* (tranquil) and *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) is found in the case of the Blessed One...
It is true that the women of the great seer Vyāsa are enchanting, and it is true that his riches are delightful;
yet, life is indeed as fickle as the flickering side-glances of an intoxicated woman.

In this work, the Blessed One, intent on the welfare of living beings, established the *śāntarasa* (the sentiment of peace) as the primary element (*aṅgin*) in his instruction capable of leading to liberation. Since the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment is undesirable to those already possessed by passion, he employed the "sugar-candy trick for children" to bring *śṛṅgāra* into the role of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the sake of gladdening the minds of all people. Ultimately, by concluding with the demonstration of impermanence—“Life is fickle”—he has elevated the supreme propriety of the *śānta* itself to the highest degree. An example of the relationship between the subordinate and primary elements (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) of the *bībhatsa* (disgust) and *śṛṅgāra* sentiments is found in my *Bauddhāvadānakalpalatā*.
Like a female jackal clinging to the neck of an intoxicated elephant that remains motionless, her heart swiftly captivated,
she moves about— her passion made manifest by blood— as she traces the marks of her fingernails and teeth.
Having repeatedly tasted his petal-like lower lip, she leaves behind the scars of her tooth-wounds.
In this amorous act at the moment of union, she reveals the height of her excessive impetuosity.

Here, through the employment of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *upamā* (simile), two mutually contradictory meanings are brought to an equal status; yet, in the conjunction of the *vībhatsa* (the loathsome) and *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) sentiments as subordinate and principal elements respectively, the female jackal—having suddenly seized the heart of the young corpse which stood motionless like one intoxicated, or having drawn it from the funeral pyre—is clinging to its neck, her longing intensely manifested in her craving for blood, or her passion clearly revealed by her red hue; scratching with her claws and tasting the lower lip marked by her teeth, she performs the act of severing limbs as if it were the act of amorous enjoyment.
Or, it reveals the excellence of her skill in lovemaking through the upward pulling of his limbs that have become stuck;

thus, while the two sentiments of the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) are equal, by the omission of the word "lady" (*kāminī*) and the use of the term "jackal" (*jambukī*) as the sole agent, the loathsome sentiment becomes predominant. Since the erotic sentiment has thereby subsided, for the speaker—the Bodhisattva—whose mind is permeated by the deep-seated impression of renunciation, this mockery of the pleasure of a woman with broad hips, through the loathing appropriate to such a thing, attains a beauty of propriety (*aucitya*). Even though, in this great sentence...
Although tranquility (*śānta*) alone is predominant [in this context], nevertheless, in the illustrative verse, it is the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) that is emphasized.
As for *vīra* (the heroic) and *karuṇa* (the pathetic), as in my *Munimatamīmāṃsā*:

"For him who was devoted to wiping the sweat from his *gāṇḍīva* bow, and who, having bathed in tears, now fiercely bears a fire of grief even more intense than the conflagration of the *khāṇḍava* forest..."
For a long time, as Abhimanyu was being severed by the rising youth of Arjuna’s son, the cry "Alas, my child!
became a muttered prayer for the rite of exorcism commenced by the slaughter of Jayadratha.

In this regard, it has been previously stated that for the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, who had gone to the battle of the Trigartas, whose son had been slain at the onset of his fresh youth, and who—wiping away the tears from his bowstring and bathed in flowing tears—bore the fire of grief, there occurred for a long time a silent recitation (*japa*) of "Alas, my son! initiated as a magical rite (*abhicāra*) for the slaying of Jayadratha.

In that [work], through the description of the vows appropriate for initiation at the destruction of the enemy, the intensity of the fire of grief, and the invocation of the term "Khāṇḍava," the Heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) is manifested; yet, when the Guest sentiment of Pathos (karuṇarasa) suddenly blazes forth with the mention of the performance of a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) for the slaughter of Saindhava, it reaches a state of supreme propriety (*aucitya*) through its ultimate resolution in valor.
This is as in my own [verse] regarding the sentiments of Tranquility, Love, Pathos, and Disgust: "With hearts wounded by the sharp side-glances of women, [the arrows] appear smeared with blood..."

Behold, those of dull intellect, afflicted by intense swelling caused by the multitude of cruel diseases such as anger and the like, being devoured by their own body-born sons— like worms clinging fast through the moisture of fat— as their bodies lie fallen upon the bed of the afflictions of saṃsāra, sink into despair.

In this context, the sharp side-glances of a woman—which serve as the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) for the tranquil sentiment (*śānta-rasa*)—become the causes of its arousal. Through the employment of words such as "son" and so forth, which resemble worms clinging to the moisture of affection in a heart wounded by the pain of grief, the sentiments of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) appear before the tranquil sentiment; with their functions stilled through complete withdrawal, they display the highest propriety (*aucitya*), like servants [in attendance]. To demonstrate that these [other sentiments] must invariably be present in the conflict of sentiments (*rasasaṅgara*), he says: "As in Amaruka’s [verse]:
'If it is indeed certain that you must go, alas, you will go; why this haste?'"
"Please stand still for just two or three steps so that I may behold your face;
for in this life, which is as fleeting as water trickling from a water-clock's channel,
who knows whether there will be another meeting with you or not?"

In this context, regarding the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) which is the subject of the section and which expands with unrestrained throat-longing as [the poet] says "I behold her face," there is an excessive impropriety excited by its connection to the dominant sentiment. This occurs because the tranquil sentiment (*śānta*), which is naturally opposed to it, has been relegated to a subordinate role; and because the erotic sentiment is rendered subordinate by the description of the vast and impermanent nature of existence, which induces world-weariness (*vairāgya*). Indeed, by hearing of the worthlessness and lack of beauty in saṃsāra, even those whose hearts are hardened by cruel deeds find their limbs become languid and weary due to the shattering of their resolve.

How much more so for those who possess a mind tender with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) as delicate as a flower—those who are full of aesthetic grace? In the end, through the fulfillment of a perfected tranquility (*śānta*), the distaste for passion (*rāga*) alone remains, like water in a parched desert.
Thus it was said by Ānandavardhana:
Whether it be contradictory or non-contradictory, a rasa must not be allowed to reach full development when another rasa is the primary element; by this means, there shall be no conflict.

That very same principle is observed here in its reverse form: even when there is a reversal of intensification (*paripoṣa*)—that is, when it is contrary to its own nature—there is still no contradiction with the primary element (*pradhāna*). As in the case of Rājaśekhara:
"Enjoy pride; cast waves of glances upon your beloveds; let youth pass for five days; and maintain the firmness of your full breasts.
Thus, as if whispering sweetly through the cuckoo's song, the God of the Five Arrows spoke to the Goddess.
O you who possess all virtues, you have been suddenly won over by the great festival of my heart; command me, everything is yours.
"Abandon pride; cast a glance more wave-like than before upon your beloved;
let youth—which stiffens the pillars of your full breasts—last for ten or fifteen days.
Thus, under the guise of the sweet warbling of the cuckoo, the command of the five-arrowed God was suddenly issued as a great festival, scraping away all [inhibitions]. (This is the shadow-text.)

"Abandon your pride toward your beloved; behold the river of youth, which lasts but five or ten days and serves to stiffen the swelling breasts"—thus speaks the Lord through the sweet warbling of the cuckoo.

In the statement, "As if by the command of the five-arrowed god (Kāma), the spring festival has bestowed its all-consuming [power]," the *mukha* (opening) sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra*), which pervades from its inception until its conclusion, is not rendered tasteless by the *bindu* (sub-episode) of tranquility (*śānta*)—which consists of impermanence and lasts for only a few days—even though it is perceived as being of the nature of spring. This is because there is no full development of that which is opposed to it. For when the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is struck by impropriety arising from the description of something contradictory, it is like an elephant fallen into a pit; it does not dare to rise again. Enough of this elaboration.
In this manner, the elephant among the wise should himself investigate the propriety of the various manifestations of differentiation within the battle of aesthetic flavors (rasa). || 18 ||

Immediately after the consideration of propriety regarding aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), in order to demonstrate the propriety of the verbal action (*kriyā*) following the sequence of the enumeration, he says:

"The possession of qualities, the excellence of meter, and grammatical correctness shine forth in poetry, just as they do in a virtuous man, provided that the action is characterized by propriety. (19)

The presence of qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) in poetry, its excellence in fine meters like *vasantatilakā* and *tilakā*, and its perfection in possessing all the required characteristics shine forth when the verb is employed with propriety (*aucitya*), just as it does for a virtuous person; thus, their similarity is self-evident. An example of propriety regarding the verb is found in my *Nītilatā*: "He who is renowned for his speed in the constant performance of the seven-ocean twilight worship..."
Is that Bālin not remembered— he who, with his great pride, brought Dundubhi to the state of a black crow,
who crushed the illusory Māyāvin to make the netherworld (Pātāla) out of his blood,
and who was skilled at plundering the splendor from the foremost of Sugrīva?

In this context, by means of the verb "is he remembered?", it is expressed through a fitting argument that Śuka and Sāraṇa— whose speed was renowned for performing worship at the seven oceans during twilight and who crushed the Dānava Dundubhi in the form of a buffalo— were cast into the armpit with their bodies confined within a corner of his garment as a beneficial counsel to turn back Rāvaṇa, who was intent on wicked conduct, after they had emerged from Pātāla filled with the blood of slaughtered Dānavas and Bhūtas.
But it is not like that of the illustrious Pravarasena, who [described] the heaven as being without the *pārijāta* tree, the moon as lacking the beauty of the *kaustubha* gem,
and the mass of Shiva’s matted locks as appearing before the churning of the ocean.
To present an example of the impropriety of a verb, he says: "But not as... (*na tu yathā*). [The verse begins:
"Svargaṃ..."—[meaning] "Heaven, devoid of the *pārijāta* tree; the chest of Madhumathana, bereft of the Kaustubha gem and Lakṣmī."
I remember the mass of Shiva’s matted hair, which is like the young moon that emerged from the churning of the nectar of immortality.

Thus ends the shadow-verse (*chāyā*). Here, while Jāmbavanta is speaking, he mentions the chest of Madhumathana (Viṣṇu) as being devoid of the *apārijāta* tree, the Kaustubha gem, and Lakṣmī, and the mass of Śiva’s matted hair as being without the young moon even before the churning for nectar. In this context of describing such excellent qualities, by means of the verb alone, only the state of his body being utterly worn out by old age is conveyed; however, no particular excellence or superiority of prowess is appropriately indicated. || 19 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of grammatical factors (kāraka), he says:
A sentence shines when its constituent parts are appropriate, just as the prosperity of a noble family is adorned by deeds of magnanimity. (20)
A sentence always shines when its constituent parts are properly inflected, just as sovereignty adorned by those born of noble lineage shines through virtuous conduct;
this is illustrated by the propriety of the agentive case in the works of Bhaṭṭa Bāṇa.
The pair of breasts of your enemies' wives, bathed in tears and situated close to the fire of grief in their hearts,
moves about without ornaments as if performing a vow of penance.
In this case, whereas one ought to say, "The wives of the enemy are observing a vow," by stating instead, "The pair of breasts, bathed in tears,
tormented by the fire of grief, having abandoned food, and devoid of pearl necklaces, performs the vow"— the subject term (*kartṛpada*) generates an appropriate sense of propriety.
It is not as in the example of Parimala.
He takes no food, he drinks no water, he does not consort with women; he sleeps upon sands and, having abandoned the objects of the senses, he endures the fierce heat of the sun.
In that desert, he is intent on obtaining even a single drop of the grace from the lotus-feet of Your Majesty.
I believe, O Lion of Mālava, that the Lord of Gujarāt is performing severe penance!

Regarding the statement here that "the Lord of Gurjara, having fled, entered a desert thicket, abandoned all objects of sense such as food, and practiced penance while enduring the fierce heat," nothing is perceived that accords with a specific intention for the subject (*kartṛpada*). Because he was distressed by the fear of his enemy and settled within the wilderness of the desert, deprived of the enjoyment of all sensual pleasures, what else could he have done? Nothing has been stated regarding the subject that is worthy of producing aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), such as would be appropriate for a pair of breasts.
An example of the propriety of the object (*karmapada*) is found in my *Lāvaṇyavatī*:
He who always possesses coolness, is accustomed to streams of pure water, and flows with great splendor, falling upon the mountain peaks; he,
possessing the luster of a fresh blue lotus to the ears of the Goddess of Fortune, displays his valor.
Your sword becomes a wondrous thing for enemies, possessing the heat of a blazing fire.

In this regard, it is truly a marvel that your sword—which possesses a steady, stainless stream of water (or coolness), sharpness, and coldness; which has the splendor of thick clouds (or dense enthusiasm) and an arising like that of a rain-cloud; and which, like a mountain, strikes down armies along with their leaders—carries the beauty of valor like a fresh blue lotus to the ears of the foe, yet causes them torment. For as it has been said, this torment, which is the object of the action, arises from a collection of causes that are themselves exceedingly cooling.
A delightful variety of propriety has been woven here;
it is not as in my own *Avasarasāra*,
where [the hero] is awakened by the wind of the sighs of his defeated enemies.
Having suddenly attained great increase by taking refuge in the fuel of wood,

and being awakened here by the wind of the sighs of fleeing enemies, your majesty— like a fire that has reached maturity in filling the circle of the quarters by relying on its fuel— spreads only heat among the wives of your foes;
thus, there is nothing surprising about this being entirely appropriate.
O Lord of the World, Your majesty, possessing the brilliance of fire, spreads heat among the wives of Your slain enemies.

In this case, your majesty’s valor—which is awakened by the wind of the sighs of terrified enemies, which attains full maturity by taking refuge in the quarters and filling the circle of the horizons, and which is equal to fire—produces only heat for the wives of your foes;
therefore, there is nothing surprising about that.

An example of propriety regarding the instrument (*karaṇaucitya*) is found in the case of the potter of Gauḍa: * *gauḍakumbhakārasya* (of the potter of Gauḍa) (Note: The specific verse illustrating this would follow, but as it was not provided in the source text, the example is indicated by its attribution.)
The sun was encircled by his tail, the moon was pierced through by his crest,
the clouds were shaken off by his mane,

and the stars were crushed between his tusks; the ocean was crossed by Hari with a mere glance, and the vast fire of his majesty was leaped over in every direction by the surging waves of his loud, boisterous laughter.

In this passage, by means of numerous instrumental words imbued with energy—acting like steps for ascending the pinnacle of wonder—the extraordinary propriety of the Son of the Wind (Hanumān) is revealed as he proclaims his victory in the undertaking of the Lord of the Raghus’ power: the ocean was encircled by Hanumān’s tail during the crossing of the sea; the moon was pierced by the edge of his crown; the clouds were shaken off by his mane; the stars were distressed by his tusks; and the vast fire of Rāvaṇa’s prowess was extinguished by his mere glance, accompanied by waves of boisterous laughter. (Note: The term *taraṇi* here refers to the sun, which was encircled by the tail; the moon (*śaśī*) was pierced by the tip of the crown; the clouds (*meghāḥ*) were dispersed by the mane (*saṭābhiḥ*); the stars (*tārāḥ*) were tormented by the tusks (*daṃṣṭrābhiḥ*); and the ocean (*abdhiḥ*) was crossed by his glance alone, while the fire of Rāvaṇa’s pride was quelled by his loud laughter.)
But it was not as in Bāṇa’s *Kādambarī*, where it is said:
"Victorious is Upendra, who, having found his mark in an instant, pierced from afar the chest of his enemy with a single arrow red with rage—
as if the chest itself had been split by fear, naturally pale-red from the wounds."

In this regard, the statement that the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu was—as if out of fear—spontaneously split by the very wrathful, blood-red, and evil eye of the Lord Nṛsiṃha, which had found its mark in an instant, results in an excessive impropriety. This is because the spontaneous bursting of the heart belongs to the antagonist, who possesses great energy and prowess and serves as the primary instrument for inflaming the majesty of the principal hero; yet here it is attributed to the "eye" (*dṛk*) acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Thus, the resting of this [impropriety] upon the head [of the poet] is fully established.
The propriety of the recipient (*sampradāna-aucitya*) is as follows: "The earth, bounded by the four quarters of the horizon, is being established [as the recipient] for Bhaṭṭa Prabhākara;
even while we are merely speaking of her being thus established, look, our hair stands on end!"
What more need be said? Homage to that Rāmā, who was bestowed upon the Brahmin, from whom this wondrous tale emerged and into whom it has finally set.

In this context, when the messenger of Rāvaṇa requested the axe, Bhārgava said: "This axe, obtained through the grace of Hara, is not fit for gift. Therefore, that Ten-necked one should be told in my name: "The earth has been bestowed by me upon Kaśyapa; what, then, have you conquered between the netherworld and the heavens that you should be given [the earth]? This is improper for a sage devoted to the welfare of the world to grant it to a Rākṣasa who is a thorn to the three worlds.
The presentation of the world;
the appropriateness of the source (apādāna), as in the case of Mālava-rudra: "Having taken from this ocean some drops of water measured [therefrom]," and so forth.
The clouds, filling the earth while obstructing the sky with their waters,
caused the stars to tremble from the fear of being crushed by the peaks of the whirling Mount Mandara; yet,
having encountered that one woman made of water (the Milky Way), the illustrious Viṣṇu became free from sorrow throughout the three worlds.

In this regard, it has been stated that just as clouds, having obtained but a limited drop of water from this great ocean, fill the world, so too did the glorious Acyuta become possessed of fortune (*śrīmān*) upon obtaining a single female water-spirit (*jalamānuṣī*), whose pupils were trembling with fear from the impact of the peaks of the whirling Mount Mandara. By this, the unsurpassed excellence inherent in the ocean is demonstrated. Here, the phrase "from this ocean" (*etasmāj jaladheḥ*) is the very foundation of propriety (*aucitya*).
But it is not as Bhaṭṭendurāja says:
"Having taken water from all around the mouths of the rivers,
what indeed has been accomplished by this great ocean?"
It was turned into alkaline ash, offered as an oblation in the submarine fire, and cast into the hollow depths at the root of the netherworld.

Here, by the designation of a "great ocean," something is said regarding a certain person who squanders wealth acquired from others, being averse to sharing with the virtuous. Having taken water from all directions from the mouths of rivers, it has been bestowed upon unworthy recipients and thus defiled. Since one ought to say here "having taken from the rivers" (*saridbhyaḥ*), the fact that "from the mouths of the rivers" (*sarinmukhebhyaḥ*) was stated results in a lack of propriety due to the uselessness of the word *mukha*.
Propriety of location (*adhikaraṇaucitya*) is as seen in Kālidāsa’s *Kunteśvaradautyam*.

Here dwells Meru, the crest-jewel of the mountains; here are the seven other oceans, their burdens laid down; and here is this surface of the earth, resplendent with the pillar-like coils of the serpent king. This very place is the domain of those such as we are.

Here, even the Great King’s envoy, failing to obtain a seat worthy of the honor and respect due to his master at the assembly of the vassals, sat upon the ground itself due to the exigency of his mission; yet, with such boldness and gravity, he spoke as follows: "For those like us, it is only fitting to have our place upon the surface of the earth—firm as the coils of the Lord of Serpents serving as a pillar for a throne—since it is right here that the sovereign of the moving Meru is seated, along with the seven oceans; therefore, our status is indeed equal to his. This was a statement consistent with the formal requirements of diplomatic protocol.

But, O best among those who possess stability, look! By fate, for these many days, your mind has been kept in a state of agitation by your servant, just as fragrance remains present there [in the flower].
Wherever your majesty prevails, it causes pearl necklaces to fall upon the trembling breasts of the fawn-eyed women.

In this regard, as for what was said by me, your servant, concerning that region where your majesty causes necklaces to fall upon the breasts of deer-eyed women—breasts trembling with agitation—it follows from that praise of the excellence of your qualities of valor and passion that your majesty, whose expansion flows unceasingly in all directions, possesses no limitation whatsoever.

[He] has arrived. In one delimited place where I am situated—where your majesty causes the trembling of necklaces upon the slopes of young women’s breasts—a distinct characteristic is observed in another place. If your majesty were omnipresent, then instead of saying "I am situated there," which refers to a single location, [one would have to say] "everywhere. Thus, the word "there" (*tatra*) denotes a specific place.

This [usage] is not appropriate, because even a mere bandit might display such prowess in a single instance. Therefore, an impropriety is perceived here regarding the word *adhikaraṇa* (locus). In those various places where your majesty resides, it would be more fitting and logically consistent for the praise to be expressed simply as "wherever your majesty is present. || 20 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of the *liṅga*, he says:
"By means of the *liṅga* alone, which is insentient, the poem attains excellence, just as the body [attains excellence] through auspicious marks that indicate majesty. (21)
A poem attains excellence through a grammatical gender appropriate to the subject matter, just as a body does through the possession of royal marks.
As it is said in my *Lalitaratnamālā*:
He does not touch sleep, he abandons even his fortitude, he maintains no fixed state anywhere, he knows no long discourse, he does not succumb to illness, and with his whole soul he attains bliss;
by him, through the recitation and meditation upon the hymn of praise to her virtues, has the *Ratnāvalī* been propitiated.
Being free from attachment, they do not tolerate even the mention of another's wife.

In this context, that which was said by Vidūṣaka to Susaṅgatā regarding the King of Vatsa—whose mind was distressed by separation from Ratnāvalī—and which was appropriate to his state of love: "He does not touch sleep; he abandons fortitude; he does not maintain composure; he regards long conversation as if it were pain; and he does not resort to diversion."

Without her, he—who recites her virtues, who is devoted to her speech, and who has abandoned social intercourse—cannot even tolerate the names of other women. In this context, the supreme appropriateness is established by superimposing the feminine gender upon the terms for "stability," "fortitude," "narrative," and "bliss," thereby treating them as if they were limbs of a woman.
This is not, however, like my *Nītilatā*, where [it says]: "Capable in the battle against Varuṇa, she has achieved her purpose through the destruction of heaven..."
Incapable of restraint or discipline, intent on the destruction of the wind-god,
and the bed of death for the god of wealth, this circle of my arms— fierce in its power to burn and crush— is ashamed to engage in battle with mere mortals.

Here Rāvaṇa speaks, appropriate for manifesting the fierce transformation of his indignation toward the host of monkeys: "My fierce circle of arms feels ashamed of fighting with a mere mortal—a shame that causes the collapse of the pride of the vast armies of the world-protectors, such as Varuṇa and the others. The use of the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) in this reference is intended to disparage [the opponent] who is otherwise fit for the conquest of the three worlds.
By removing the harshness of his majesty, he indicates impropriety. || 21 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of speech, he says:
"Poetry attains beauty only through appropriate words, just as the face of the wise—whose minds are blessed by freedom from wretchedness—attains beauty. (22)

Poetry attains beauty through the singular, dual, and plural numbers, just as the speech of the learned—whose minds are noble and free from wretchedness—attains beauty through words that are charming due to their propriety and elegance when making requests.
As it is said in my *Nītilatā*:
"By the conquests of the three worlds, by the victories of the Boar, and by the acquisition of countless jewels..."
Renowned for hundreds of self-chosen marriages by his own will amidst the ocean of battle,
and for his many wondrous feats of binding Bali, the son of Pulastya stands ever laughing at Hari, whose sleep is interrupted only once due to the exhaustion of his exertion.

In this context, while Śuka and Sāraṇa were describing the prowess of the Lord of the Raghus before him, it was said: "The descendant of Pulastya, renowned for his awakening from sleep upon the serpent Śeṣa due to the fatigue of yoga, is ever laughing with great enthusiasm— [a laughter] caused by his many conquests over the worlds, his victories over the great warriors who triumphed as boars, his acquisition of numerous jewels, his hundred times self-choice of Śrī amidst the ocean of battle, and his binding of Bali and the world-protectors."
By means of these very plural expressions, the propriety characterized by the distinction from Hari has been accumulated and manifested;
it is not, however, as in Mātṛgupta’s [verse]:
"This is not the royal swan of the lotus-pond at the face of night..."
O King! This moon, whose body is as lovely as the surface of Kīrī’s cheek, shines in the sky; it is indeed your fame, white as a mass of foam from the Ocean of Milk.

In this regard, as for what was stated—that "this body of yours is not fame, white like a mass of foam from the milk-ocean"—the use of the singular number is shown to be inappropriate when the description of fame, which flows in an unbroken stream, ought to be expressed by means of the plural.
To demonstrate the propriety of adjectives, he says: "The object to be qualified is made manifest by appropriate qualifiers."
One who is noble in virtue is like a virtuous person toward friends when they are superior in merit. || 23 ||
In poetry, the subject matter attains beauty only through appropriate qualifiers, just as a virtuous man, noble in his qualities, shines through friends of superior merit;
as in my *Munimatamīmāṃsā*:

In the month of Caitra, for whom is everything not most dear— the groves whose youth is manifested by the blossoming of mango trees, the fragrant lotus ponds, the palaces with their jeweled balconies draped in moonlight, and beautiful women? Yet, that which is actually enjoyed therein is what truly matters.
Life is like an unbaked earthen vessel made of clay, destined for swift destruction.

In this context, while describing the majesty and power of Yudhiṣṭhira—who had acquired great wealth and took pride in the jewel-encrusted assembly hall constructed by Maya—the opportunity arose to examine the intention of the Great Sage, who teaches the doctrine that the nature of all things consists in both existence and non-existence. It was said: "The groves, whose youthfulness is gathered in the season of flowers; the lotus ponds, beautiful with the fragrance of nectar; the palaces and jeweled turrets draped in canopies of moonlight; and lovely women—all this is exceedingly beautiful and desired by everyone."

However, that life in which one eats is as insubstantial as an unbaked earthen vessel and quickly perishes; thus, by means of the beauty expressed through the qualifying adjectives that enhance the excellence of the subject being qualified, it spreads a shimmering propriety that accords with the disillusionment arising from its ultimate worthlessness.
This is not, however, like Bhaṭṭa Laṭṭana’s [verse]:
"Let them hate the summer and long for the arrival of the clouds..."
Those lakes are narrow in nature and vast;
but of the ocean, there is a twofold inconceivability: the water in its belly remains motionless like that of the immovable Lord Indra, even while the foolish minnows dart about within it.

In this context, it is said that "let the narrow and formidable ponds, being of a precarious nature, hate the summer and long for the arrival of the clouds; but as for the great ocean—whose waters in its belly remain as still as a mountain peak despite the agitation of young fish—the summer and the arrival of the clouds are both negligible. Here, the impropriety of the two adjectives *saṅkaṭa* (narrow) and *vikaṭa* (formidable), which possess mutually contradictory meanings, clearly manifests.

For it is not possible for that which is narrow by nature to possess a wide or expansive form. If, on the other hand, narrowness were its nature and wideness its form, that too would be untenable, because a pond, being insentient, lacks an inherent nature [of such a duality]. || 23 ||
To demonstrate the nature of prefixes, he says:

"Through association with suitable prefixes, eloquent speech—already endowed with unrestrained virtues—increases in excellence, just as prosperity grows for those who have entered the path of the virtuous. (24)
Good speech attains excellence through prefixes such as *pra* and others, just as prosperity does through treading upon the path of the virtuous;
as it is said by me in the *Munimatamīmāṃsā*:

A person who has fallen from the peak of happiness and is utterly ruined adopts proper conduct yet abandons it, embraces passion yet takes hold of dispassion; desiring to perform penance that would shatter the pride as lofty as the sky born of worldly attachment, he wavers through its opposites.
For the most part, it attains a workability similar to iron melted by heat.

In this context, while describing the difficult-to-grasp state of Duryodhana— who, his pride shattered by the defeat and capture at the hands of the Gandharvas during the cattle-expedition (*ghoṣayātrā*), abandoned his vast sovereignty and devoted himself to the practice of asceticism— it was said that every person who has fallen from happiness and lost their wealth resorts to virtuous conduct and [avoids] intoxication.

He abandons [worldly life], takes recourse in dispassion (*vairāgya*), and, through the shattering of attachments, desires to perform asceticism (*tapas*) with his lofty pride dissolved; for the most part, by way of abundance, he attains a pliability (*karmaṇyatā*) like that of a mass of iron melted by heat.
