In this context, the natural excellence of the word *tuṅga* (lofty), being used as a secondary member (*ut-*) in a compound with a prefix, reaches a state of doubled intensity, which brings about the intended meaning of "excessive, intoxicated pride. It is not, however, as in the case of Kumāradāsa: [The verse of Kumāradāsa follows...]
O timid one, abandon this firm embrace;
leave your lover, O fair-limbed one! The sun’s rays are now rising, and the cocks are crowing.

In this context, regarding the awakening of the woman whose limbs were rendered motionless by the firm embrace of a fresh union with her lover, the friend said: "Release your beloved; the dawn twilight has arrived, the rays of the sun are emerging, and the cocks are now crowing. This was said merely to fill the silence, as she remained devoid of any response to the impending calamity.
Because it is devoid of meaning, it is simply inappropriate. || 24 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of particles (*nipāta*), he says:
"By means of particles placed in their appropriate positions, the coherence of the meaning becomes indeed stable, just as by means of ministers who are worthy of being employed. (25)

When particles such as *ca* and others are placed appropriately within the words, they bring about a connection of the poetic meaning that is free from doubt, just as one achieves success through the aid of good companions.
As it says in my *Munimatamīmāṃsā*:

"All those who desire the happiness of heaven perform sacrifices with abundant hundreds of rituals; yet for them, a vast amount of time passes in the city of the gods, while for [the wise], it is but half a moment."

When the wealth of merit is exhausted, stability does not remain, just as it does not for lovers in the house of a courtesan; therefore, O sirs, take refuge in that which is both true and eternal—the bliss of liberation!

In this context, once the futility and instability of the pleasure of heaven—characterized by a distasteful end—has been established, the firm conviction regarding the immovable bliss of liberation, reinforced by the use of indeclinable particles (*nipāta*), generates the propriety of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthaucitya*).
This is not as in the following example:
"The Lord knows everything; whatever we say, even that is rooted in policy."
Having made an alliance with your kinsman, the King of the Earth who wears a net-like armor, be at peace;
destroy the barbarians, shatter your infamy day by day, and encompass the entire world with your glories.
Furthermore, place your hand upon the earth girdled by the ocean.

In this context of praising the king, although it was said, "Your Majesty knows all, both that and this," the use of the word "ca" (and) is indeed meaningless and useless due to the lack of connection between what precedes and what follows; like one who has sat down unperceived in the midst of a row of many people feasting at a grand festival, he becomes manifest only later, spreading impropriety with a mind distressed by shame. || 25 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of timing, he says:
"By means of the propriety of timing, a sentence indeed attains beauty through its meaning, just as the body of the virtuous [attains beauty] through a dress that is pleasing to people. (26)

The speech of the wise, who know the proper occasion, attains beauty through a meaning endowed with appropriateness determined by time, just as their physical form does through the adoption of attire suited to the season;
as it was said by me in my *Munimatamīmāṃsā*: [text follows].

O Lord of the Universe, O Lord of Birds, O Śauri, O Murāri, O Hari! He who was once a cowherd boy, a thief of milk and curds, and a smasher of dung-heaps—today, O Śrīvatsa-marked one, [he is celebrated as] "Jahnu. With these words of praise, the ears of men are filled.
Ah! How strange is this process of ripening, which is the very opposite of the nature of time!

In this context, when Śiśupāla—desiring his own death through the manifestation of the poison of indignation—declares that he was once a cowherd boy, a thief of milk, curds, and butter, and one who scraped dried cow-dung, [Kṛṣṇa] replied: "Alas!

Oh, how wonderful is the transformative power of Time, the ground of marvelous maturation, by which the ears of people are today filled with words of praise for him by the Lord of the World and others! By using the past tense (*bhūta-kāla*), he has employed a fittingness of speech characterized by an insult, made beautiful by the satisfaction of wonder.
Or as in Mālavakuvalaya’s *Cyutāsumanasaḥ*: "The kunda trees are sluggish with the emergence of their blossoms;
and these cuckoos, though holding words in their minds, do not utter them."
And yet, the rays of the sun quiver with a cool radiance, and they do not hang heavy like withered lotuses, bringing on exhaustion.

Here, in the description of the longing of the God of Love, indicated by the fresh delight of the young springtime groves, the *kunda* flowers—appropriate to the transition between seasons—have their bodies rendered empty as their blossoms have fallen; the *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* trees are languid under the weight of emerging buds; the cuckoos in their minds pursue their sweet warbling; and the rays of the sun, while warding off the cold, do not yet assume a full intensity that would cause distress—thus it is said, using only words denoting the present tense.
A certain propriety, beautiful because it resonates with the heart, brings delight;
as in the verse of Bhūṭṭabhaṭṭa:
"This drawn bow is like the gaping mouth of Death, and these arrows are like quivering venom."
That training has been mastered by Arjuna; his movement, clinging to every limb, is now at rest.
Alas! There is a wickedness within the honey, and a captivating song on its surface; I think that as soon as this hunter speaks, the forest will be cleared of deer.

Here, the hunter’s bow, his training in archery, his movements, and his cruelty—along with his songs—are such that the forest will become devoid of deer; thus, the future tense, through the nourishment of the intended meaning, brings about a fitting resonance with the heart.
It is not, however, as in the case of Varāhamihira’s [work].
The moon, having waned, enters the orb of the sun month after month; having acquired some small portion, it follows [the sun] ever further and further away.
If it becomes full, it then rises in rivalry with the sun; yet it does not do so out of malice, nor does this dull-witted one cease its course out of wretchedness.

In this context, the moon enters the solar disc every month until it is diminished; then, having acquired some nourishing digit, it becomes increasingly distant and rises again in fullness as if in rivalry with that very same sun.

The two temporal expressions *na viramati* (does not cease) and *na ca dainyādvyaraṃsīt* (nor did it desist from wretchedness)—which are mutually inconsistent—are presented here regarding the moon's two similar acts of wickedness (*daurjanya*) that are perpetually accomplished. Among these, the term *vyaraṃsīt* is indeed improper because its meaning is contradictory [to the context]. || 26 ||
To demonstrate propriety of setting, he says:
"The meaning of a poem shines through propriety of place, accompanied by consistency, just as the conduct of the virtuous, pointing toward further intimacy, is beautiful. (27)
The meaning of poetry shines like the conduct of the virtuous, indicating intimacy through its resonance with the heart and its appropriateness to place and region;
as, for example, in that of Bhaṭṭa Bhavabhūti.
Where formerly there was a stream, now there is a sandbank; where there were rivers, now there is a reversal; the density and sparseness of the trees have changed.
After a long time, I consider this forest to be as if it were another.
The configuration of the mountains strengthens the cognition that "this is that."

Here, after many years have passed since the occasion of the slaying of Śambūka, Rāma has re-entered the Daṇḍaka forest previously cleared by him; observing it all around, he speaks thus: "Where formerly there was the flow of rivers, now there is the bank; where there was the density or sparseness of trees, the reverse has been seen after a long time."

"I consider this forest to be as if unprecedented, yet the configuration of the mountain makes me firm in the conviction that it is indeed that very same place. When this is said, the description of the forest—whose features have undergone transformation over a long period of time—resonates with the heart, and the natural character of the region illuminates the highest degree of propriety. It is not, however, as in the case of Rājaśekhara’s [work].
Struck by the side-glances of beautiful Mahārāṣṭrī women white with smiles, pressed by the breasts of mature Āndhrī women, terrified by the knitting of eyebrows by his beloveds,
entwined by the arms of Lāṭī women, and threatened by the forefinger of Malaya women— [he was thus tormented].
Thus, this very poet Rājaśekhara now desires Vārāṇasī.

When it was said, "Here, the poet Rājaśekhara— who was once rendered charming by his dalliances with the women of Karṇāṭa, Mahārāṣṭra, Andhra, Lāṭa, and Malaya, and who has now, in the course of time, lost his passion and delusion— desires to go to Vārāṇasī," there followed a description of the southern regions, where the god of love is unrestrained due to the association with beautiful women whose limbs are rippled with the sentiment of erotic love (śṛṅgārarasa).

By the word "beloved" (*praṇayinī*) alone—devoid of the qualifying term "of the region"—which would have served as a regional indicator, the phrase "terrified by the knitting of the brows of the beloved" renders even the heightened propriety of the setting inappropriate. || 27 ||
To demonstrate what is appropriate for a particular lineage, he says: "The propriety accumulated within a family is a cause of excellence;
it is generally dear to the sensitive, just as it is to a man. (28)
Just as in the case of a man, for poetry, nobility of lineage produces a particularly distinguished excellence and is generally,
for the most part, esteemed by connoisseurs;
as, for example, in the case of Kālidāsa.
Then he, his soul withdrawn from the objects of the senses, having according to the prescribed rite bestowed the white sunshade— the insignia of sovereignty— upon his young son,
took refuge in the shade of a tree in a sage’s grove together with that queen.
For this is indeed the family vow of the Ikṣvākus when their youth has faded.

Then, having entrusted the kingdom to his young son, that aged king retired to a forest of asceticism along with the queen; for it has been said that among the Ikṣvākus, whose minds are detached from worldly things, this alone is the family vow.
By this statement, the propriety of those belonging to that lineage—past, present, and future—is revealed.
But it is not as in the case of King Yaśovarman,
whose birth was in a family of jesters, yet he attained his desired position;
nevertheless, even such enjoyments cannot be experienced even once by chance.

"In this regard, my birth in the family of Bhaṇḍa was intended, and likewise the attainment of the desired status has been accomplished; nevertheless, due to separation from my beloved bestowed by fate, these enjoyments cannot be experienced"—when this is stated, the "family of Bhaṇḍa," which is personally known [to the speaker] but unknown elsewhere, is pointed out by the mere mention of a word devoid of any specific excellence. Thus, due to its lack of meaning, it is indeed improper. However, the absence of qualifiers for the Ikṣvāku family is quite appropriate, because its conduct is universally renowned throughout the three worlds as being consistent with propriety. (28)
To demonstrate the propriety of the vow, he says:
"The meaning of the poem, consisting of words of praise, through the weight of its propriety toward the noble vow, fills the minds of people with devotion and an abundance of contentment. (29)

The meaning of a poem, through the dignity of its appropriately observed vows, becomes worthy of praise from the virtuous and fills the minds of people with satisfaction. This is the interruption of devotion (*bhaktivicchitti*).
As in my own *Muktāvalī* poem:
Here, the leafy trees, clad in bark and adorned with the ashes of the abundance of flower-pollen,
shine like ascetics who wear bracelets of restless bees as their rosaries.

In this description of the feet—adorned with bark garments, ashes, rosaries, and the like, which manifest the vows of one whose wealth is asceticism—even an insentient object is brought to a state of propriety through the mental disposition appropriate to the occasion of tranquility.
It is not, however, as in the case of the *dīpaka* (lamp) [simile]:
"In a holy village or a great forest, taking a skull-bowl covered with a white cloth, [he sits] near the smoke of the sacrificial fire offered by twice-born men who are filled with righteousness."
It is better for a proud creature, afflicted by hunger, to wander from door to door to fill the cavernous pit of its belly than to be wretched every day among one's own kin.

In this description of unimpeded dispassion, it is better that a proud man, emaciated by hunger, takes up his mendicant’s bowl and sets out to fill his belly, wandering from door to door with a staff in hand, rather than [entering the palace].

Furthermore, when told that his kinsmen are in distress, he abandons the contentment found in the rest of a mind purified by innate tranquility, and instead utters words solely intent on hatred toward his kin and the desire for victory—utterances that manifest extreme impropriety. "Better this hardship of severe ascetic vows than hearing the wretchedness of one's own people"—this is the casting off of the pride that binds one to the knots of worldly existence. (29)
To demonstrate the variety of reality (tattva-vaicitrya), he says:
"Poetry that resonates with the heart, through the certainty of conviction in truth, attains the status of being accepted or rejected by the poet via expressions appropriate to that reality. (30)
A poet’s well-spoken verse attains the status of a reliable testimony through an account consistent with reality;
as in my *Bauddhāvadānakalpalatā*:
Whether in heaven or on earth, among the hosts of serpents, in childhood or youth, in old age or at the time of death, or while resting in the bed of the womb—
for those embodied beings who are capable of departing together [with their loved ones] in every way—
For there is no destruction of past karma.

Here, by stating that there is no destruction of past karma because it is capable of accompanying embodied beings through the three worlds and through the stages of childhood, youth, and old age, the author demonstrates the propriety of proclaiming a truth that is unanimously confirmed in the hearts of all people without doubt;
it is not, however, as in the case of Māgha’s [verse].

The rays of light are not devoured by those seeking food, nor is the essence of poetry drunk by those who thirst for it; no one has ever raised up their lineage through learning. Therefore, acquire gold alone; the arts are fruitless.

In this regard, by the statement, "Seek wealth alone, for it is directed toward the attainment of all goals; hunger does not eat without food, nor is the essence of poetry drunk by the thirsty, and no one has ever uplifted a family through learning alone," everything presented here is devoid of truth, contrary to fact, and improper, as it concerns one whose fortitude has been shattered by the wretchedness of poverty. It is only those who possess learning—which spreads like a creeper of all prosperity—that have the capacity to uplift a family, and no one else. (30)
To demonstrate the diversity of character (*sattva*), he says:
"The speech of a poet that is appropriate to his character certainly produces wonder, like the conduct of a wise man who is reflective, charming, and noble. (31)
The speech of a poet, when appropriate to its subject, produces aesthetic wonder, just as the noble conduct of a wise man appears beautiful when reflected upon;
as seen in my play, the *Citrabhāratī*.
His body was filled with the waters flowing freely from a multitude of rivers, yet his water was consumed by the dense submarine fire of blazing, swelling flames;

possessing great self-control, he experienced neither pride nor dejection. Indeed, for the great, there is no transformation caused by the diversity of circumstances, even when they have drunk up the waters.

Here, while describing the excellence of Yudhiṣṭhira’s character through the metaphor of the ocean, it is stated that the ocean—vast in its essence—experiences neither overflow nor contraction when its body is swollen by the rising of rivers or drunk up by the submarine fire; for great-souled beings do not undergo transformation merely due to changes in circumstances. Thus, a profound and steady disposition of character establishes propriety. This is not as in the case of Bhaṭṭendurāja: [The verse of Bhaṭṭendurāja follows: "O Ocean, you have drunk the waters of the Gaṅgā; you have swallowed the submarine fire; you have held the earth upon your lap; and you have even borne the weight of the world. Yet, O Lord, you remain the same, whether the moon rises or sets. In this [verse], the description of the ocean's greatness is rendered inappropriate because it is based on a mere enumeration of external conditions. It does not convey the intended meaning of the ocean’s inherent nature. Therefore, the former example is superior. Furthermore, in the following verse, the description of the ocean’s greatness is expressed through the metaphor of a king: "The ocean, though its body is increased by the swelling of rivers and yet drunk up by the submarine fire, experiences neither pride nor contraction, being vast in its essence. For those of noble mind do not undergo change due to the diversity of circumstances. By stating this, the profound and steady conduct of character displays propriety. It is not, however, as in the verse of Bhaṭṭendurāja: [The verse of Bhaṭṭendurāja follows: "O Ocean, you have drunk the waters of the Gaṅgā; you have swallowed the submarine fire; you have held the earth upon your lap; and you have even borne the weight of the world. Yet, O Lord, you remain the same, whether the moon rises or sets. In this [verse], the description of the ocean's greatness is rendered inappropriate because it is based on a mere enumeration of external conditions. It does not convey the intended meaning of the ocean’s inherent nature. Therefore, the former example is superior. Moreover, in the following verse, the description of the ocean’s greatness is expressed through the metaphor of a king: "The king, though his body is increased by the swelling of rivers [revenues] and yet drained by the submarine fire [the army], experiences neither pride nor contraction, being vast in his essence. For those of noble mind do not undergo change due to the diversity of circumstances. By stating this, the profound and steady conduct of character displays propriety. It is not, however, as in the verse of Bhaṭṭendurāja: [The verse of Bhaṭṭendurāja follows: "O King, you have drunk the waters of the Gaṅgā [your enemies]; you have swallowed the submarine fire [your own troops]; you have held the earth upon your lap; and you have even borne the weight of the world. Yet, O Lord, you remain the same, whether the moon [your enemy] rises or sets. In this [verse], the description of the king's greatness is rendered inappropriate because it is based on a mere enumeration of external conditions. It does not convey the intended meaning of the king’s inherent nature. Therefore, the former example is superior. Thus, the description of the ocean’s greatness through the metaphor of a king is more effective than the description of the ocean’s greatness through the metaphor of the ocean itself. This is because the former conveys the intended meaning of the king’s inherent nature, whereas the latter does not. Therefore, the former is superior. Furthermore, in the following verse, the description of the ocean’s greatness is expressed through the metaphor of a king: "The king, though his body is increased by the swelling of rivers [revenues] and yet drained by the submarine fire [the army], experiences neither pride nor contraction, being vast in his essence. For those of noble mind do not undergo change due to the diversity of circumstances. By stating this, the profound and steady conduct of character displays propriety. It is not, however, as in the verse of Bhaṭṭendurāja: [The verse of Bhaṭṭendurāja follows: "O King, you have drunk the waters of the Gaṅgā [your enemies]; you have swallowed the submarine fire [your own troops]; you have held the earth upon your lap; and you have even borne the weight of the world. Yet, O Lord, you remain the same, whether the moon [your enemy] rises or sets."
How marvelous is that blessed submarine fire, and how marvelous the ocean, contemplating whose extraordinary deeds a trembling arises in the mind!
For the one who devours the depths, no satisfaction arose despite drinking the waters; for the other, the Great Soul, not even the slightest fatigue was produced in his body.

In this context, regarding the greatness of the essence (*sattva*) of both the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) and the ocean as it will be described: since the former drinks [the water] with a capacity that is not very vast, no satisfaction arises from the waters; yet for the latter, who is dependent upon them, there is not even the slightest weariness. When it is said that both of these are wonders, one might ask: "To whom would the submarine fire not feel shame due to its lack of contentment and constant [craving], and to whom would the ocean not possess the power to fulfill the needs of those who depend on it? Thus, praising the essence of one who lacks essence brings about impropriety. || 31 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of intention, he says:
"A well-spoken word that supports one's intention, when delivered without distress, surely wins over the hearts of the virtuous, just as straightforwardness wins over those who are at ease. (32)
Poetry that effortlessly fulfills one's intentions captivates the heart, just as stainless cleansing does for virtuous people;
as in the case of a lamp.
With his left hand torn by the talons of a hawk and the space between his forearm and elbow scarred by the bowstring,
with the corners of his eyes, hands, feet, and face darkened by the smoke of fire, and possessing a broad chest—
O Mother, I believe this prince, though standing amidst the twice-born, is somehow free from all taint.
O daughter, if this distinguished guest has thus entered your womb through his own meritorious deeds;

In this context, a woman who takes pleasure in her own will, seeing a handsome young traveler at the close of day, speaks thus to her mother to indicate her intention: "This man, who has the appearance of a prince and is well-versed in the use of falcons, snares, and arrows, has arrived at evening. When this was said, the mother, fulfilling his desire, replied: "Daughter, if that is so, let him enter the inner chamber; for a distinguished guest who has arrived through the power of past merits is to be honored.
By this, a propriety that clearly indicates her intention and is enriched by aesthetic fitness shines forth.
But it was not as you were distressed for the sake of this very husband of yours, O lady whose mind was distracted by separation, that you suddenly fell at the feet of Caṇḍikā;
for even though your forehead was crushed by the tip of the umbrella atop the incense-burner which you yourself had placed there, I did not perceive it at all.

In this context, when her friend, after a long time, spoke words intended to conceal the scar from the nail-mark on her forehead—saying, "O you who are maddened by separation! You did not notice that your own forehead was wounded by the tip of the incense burner which you yourself placed there while prostrating at your husband's feet"—[the husband] said: "O you who are crazed by longing! While you were prostrating at my feet for my sake, you did not realize that your forehead had been marked by the edge of the incense burner you yourself had set down."
Only her own voluntary concealment and instruction are observed; there is no particular intention on the part of either her or her friend. || 32 ||

To demonstrate the nature of intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*), he says: The appropriateness of intrinsic essence shines forth as the beautiful ornament of well-spoken words, being unartificial and unique, just like the natural beauty (*lāvaṇya*) of women. (33)
Just as at the end of my meditation on the Sage’s teaching, a woman— her hair-tip dripping with water,
her breasts covered by a necklace-like [silk cloth], her skin bristling with goosebumps and sighing from the cold;
her eyes red at the corners from washed-away collyrium— at the conclusion of her bath, [is seen by me].
Whose heart is not made moist with longing by her flowing mass of braided hair?

In this context, while Śuka, the son of Vyāsa—who was free from attachment due to his profound dispassion—was bathing and emerging on the banks of the celestial Gaṅgā, he beheld the goddesses of the thirty [heavens] stripped of their garments and unabashed at being seen; yet, with a mind purified by tranquility, he remained unmoved by the onset of passion. As drops of water fell from the ends of their curls drawn back to their ears onto their breasts, creating for a moment the illusion of pearl necklaces, they were cooled by that [water].

"Whose heart would not be moistened with longing by this young woman who has just emerged from her bath—her body bristling with thrills, her eyes reddened at the corners by washed-off collyrium, and her mass of hair flowing loose? When this was said, it is fitting to remark that "one whose own nature is moist [with compassion] moistens even another"; yet it is not as in my own verse on that same subject:
Devotion [leads to] cowardice; forbearance to fearfulness; praise of the venerable to wretchedness; fortitude to cruelty; intellect to crookedness; learning to instability;
meditation to deceitfulness; austerity to hypocrisy; and the vow of virtuous conduct to impotence.
What indeed does not become stained with fault by the words of those who observe the vow of backbiting?

In this context, while describing the nature of the slanderer and establishing the opposite qualities of virtues such as devotion, it is stated: "How could the words of slanderers not become moistened by defects? [The response is:
For one whose own nature is inherently dry, it is indeed improper to attempt to make them wet. || 33 ||

In order to demonstrate the appropriateness of this compendium of essentials, he says by way of a summary statement: "The meaning of poetry, when its fruit is certain, is approved by whom it is not—like an operation that does not involve procrastination? (34)
To whom is the meaning of a poem not pleasing when its fruit is well-ascertained through a summary statement, like the action of one who acts swiftly?
As in my *Munimatamīmāṃsā*:

The sages, burdened by the weight of various dense collections of internal knots [of doctrine], have adhered to nothing that is the true reality. This essence, which has been made the object of beautiful reflection, belongs to the Great Seer; "I am" is the ground of worldly existence, while "I am not" is indeed liberation.

In this investigation of the meaning of the Bhagavadgītā, a compendium of the essence has been set forth: namely, that among the various doctrines produced by the scriptures of many different schools, there is nothing said by those of fixed intellect who are obsessed with them that constitutes the essential truth to be accepted. Rather, it is this alone which is the firm conclusion reached through the pure inquiry of the wise and great seer Vyāsa: that egoism is the root-ground of transmigratory existence, and that liberation consists solely in the total renunciation of the sense of "mine-ness. This brief instruction on the destruction of fear nourishes the supreme appropriateness of the subject at hand;
it does not do so in the manner of a mere wandering mendicant.

Austerity was not practiced; we ourselves were the ones who practiced it. Pleasures were not enjoyed; we ourselves were the ones who enjoyed them. Old age did not decay; we ourselves have grown old. Thirst did not depart; we ourselves have departed.
To demonstrate the propriety of inspired genius (*pratibhā*), he says:
"The poet's poem, when adorned with genius, shines with appropriateness, just as the stainless family of a virtuous man is graced by prosperity. (35)
O merciless one! Why do you bite my lower lip, mistaking it for a bimba fruit? O fair-complexioned one, become hopeless regarding ripe jambu fruits like mine, Lāvaṇyavatī.
Thus perceiving that her beloved had arrived at the doorway, another woman,
whose lip was bitten by her lover's teeth, spoke to the parrot in low, sweet tones.

In this context, a certain woman, having learned that her beloved had arrived at the entrance of the door, bit her lip with the teeth of a forest-dwelling lover; yet, as if ignorant of his arrival, she spoke auspicious words. By saying, "Why do you tear at my lower lip out of greed for the *bimba* fruit? O restless one, now lose hope for the ripe *jambū* fruits!

I am angry and will not give them to you," she creates a marvelous charm through the propriety of her speech—a cleverness of intellect characterized by ever-new flashes of wit and the skillful concealment of her true intent. As it has been said:
Bhaṭṭa Tauta maintains that *pratibhā* (creative intuition) is wisdom characterized by ever-new manifestations;
it is not, however, as I [hold] in that very same work:
"When the beloved has departed from the house, when the bed has been made, and when the floral offerings have been laid aside..."

When the morning arrived and the sun, red with passion, had ascended the mountain of dawn, she—her eyes fixed on the door, distressed and alone—cried out, "It is too early! and by tugging at the hem of his garment and striking him with her feet, she turned that lover into a *aśoka* tree (red with blossoms).

In this scene, a courtesan, having completed her turn with a lover who had been attached to her, spent the night with a new suitor. At dawn, when he had departed, the former lover arrived—his desire for union with her having been thwarted by the marks of her recent dalliance with another, such as the remains of the bedding—and was enraged by the deception of his turn. His mind seized by the grip of intense passion, he approached her; she, longing to behold you and distressed, cast her eyes toward the door and said, "I am alone and asleep," her words faltering as she tried to convince him. Yet, as he prepared to drag her away with impetuous and passionate force, she acted out of jealous anger.

The meaning of the sentence—that [the tree] was made *aśoka* (free from sorrow) by the blows of his lotus-like feet, rendered *niḥśoka* (devoid of thorns/sorrow) by the uprooting of the shafts of doubt, and brought to a state equal to the *aśoka* tree because of its constant bristling with horripilation—is merely stated; it does not suggest even a grain of propriety arising from poetic intuition (*pratibhā*). || 35 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of the situation, he establishes that propriety:
"Poetry attains honor in the world by possessing the appropriateness of its circumstances, just as an action that is beautiful when scrutinized is worthy of being performed by the wise. (36)
Poetry attains praise in the world by virtue of its appropriateness to the situation, just as the action of the wise is resplendent with the brilliance of deliberation;
as in my *Lāvaṇyavatī*.

The playful tossing of the ball has ceased, and the flickering restlessness appropriate to childhood has vanished; her artless innocence is cast aside as she adopts the gait of an elephant, and she practices the dancing of her eyebrows.
The fawn-eyed maiden has fashioned within herself a divine eloquence of wit; thus, the entire weight of her charming pride and coquettish grace is now firmly established in her words.

In this regard, since it has been said that ball-playing was abandoned, childhood fickleness discarded, artlessness cast aside, the gait of an elephant adopted, the practice of the dance of the eyebrows undertaken, and the variety of speech in jests initiated— by this we know that she is casting off the stage of childhood.

When it is said, "Though she has not yet attained maturity, this young girl has assumed the full weight [of womanhood] through a charming sense of self-importance, pregnant with the dignity of her first experience of love," a certain propriety seems to flash forth in the description of the transition between the intermediate stages of youth;
such is not the case, however, in the work of Rājaśekhara.
The elder brother, a bowman who held a new bow in his hand,
was accompanied by one whose belly was as dark as a cloud, who was skilled in the crushing of the Kṣatriyas, and who had struck down Tāṭakā and Tāḍaka;
he was joined by one with grey hair shimmering at the edge of his ears, yet possessing the voice of a suckling child.
"How is it that the son of Jamadagni does not feel shame now, desiring to fight?

Here stands Bhārgava, advanced in old age, yet possessing firm prowess and pride in his mastery of the bow; how can he, with his hair white at the temples, not feel shame as he wishes to fight with this child Rāma, whose tender lotus-hands are reddened by grasping the bow, who is arrogant in his fury for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, and whose throat still throbs with drops of his mother’s breast-milk?"—when this was said, the contrast between the delicate state of the descendant of Raghu and the aged state of the son of Jamadagni was established.
The sense of dwelling in opposition, expressed as "Tāṭakā and Tāḍaka," produces a certain contraction in the mind due to its impropriety. || 36 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of critical inquiry, he says:
"Well-spoken words attain beauty through appropriate investigation, just as the sciences of the wise reach perfection through the realization of the true nature of what is to be known. (37)
Well-spoken words attain beauty through the propriety of their deliberation, just as the learning of the wise does through knowledge of the true nature of what is to be known;
as it was said by me, while striving for truth, at the time of explaining the term *adhvatraya* in my *Munimatamīmāṃsā*:
That which was uttered by the son of Dharma with false and crooked words— “He is an elephant”—

I suspect is the unfolding of the Fortune of the Goddess Śrī, who, though her onset is darkened by taking refuge in the lotus, always indicates through that very falsehood an incomparable and true radiance.

In this narrative of Droṇa’s death, when the son of Dharma— who was possessed of the resolve for truthful conduct— spoke falsely with light words, saying "it is an elephant," that speech resulted in the final attainment of the fruit through the realization of the truth, rooted in the contemplation of the nature of Fortune (Śrī) herself; for Fortune, who constantly manifests a hatred for the moon of truth, had expanded her dark activities by taking refuge in the lotus [of Yudhiṣṭhira], and this statement served as a confirmation of that very nature.
Deliberation reveals propriety as something to be experienced by those with refined sensibilities;
it is not, however, as in my own verse at that very same place: "When the long-past dragging of the hair and garments of my beloved was still fresh..."
If this cruel slaughter of a Rākṣasa was committed by Bhīma against Duḥśāsana,
why did he endure that for so long while living in exile in the wilderness, harsh with grass and stones? Did he drink water mixed with the sweat of the buffaloes scorched by the intense heat?

In this account of Bhīmasena’s deeds, when it is considered that Bhīma committed a terrible demonic act against Duḥśāsana—following the humiliation of Draupadī’s hair-pulling after thirteen years had passed—if that was done by one who forgave an offense committed so recently, then what was the point of his long residence in the forest, which was as harsh as thorny grass, needles, and jagged stones?
It is like drinking water mixed with the sweat of a buffalo submerged in the heat of summer; thus, an improper action has been described.
Because there is an absence of investigation into the cause and because it is groundless, this groundless objection leads to an impropriety. || 37 ||
To demonstrate the propriety of names, he says:
"By its name, which corresponds to its action, the manifestation of the merits and defects of a poem is known, just as that of a person, in accordance with [their] correspondence. (38)
Just as in Kālidāsa’s [work]: "Even at first, this five-arrowed god (Kāma), irresistible because of my longing for an object so difficult to obtain, consumes my mind."
How much more so when sprouts are displayed by mango trees whose leaves are shaken by the Malaya breezes?

In this case, at the very outset, my mind—rendered irresistible by the longing for an object so difficult to attain—is being shattered by the five-arrowed god; how much more so when the sprouts are displayed upon the mango trees of the pleasure garden, shaken by the Malaya breeze? When this was said, it was indeed appropriate to call the god of love "the five-arrowed one. Or as in my *Bauddhāvadānalatā*:

Having drunk up her childhood through youth, she became the enemy of the God of Love; with the grace of her limbs, she became the companion of the movement of every part of her body, accepted by the ocean of beauty.
Without the exertion of vast waves, her prowess was free from agitation.
By her, the Lord whose weapon is his playful grace conquers the sovereignty of the worlds.

In this regard, it was said: "By that slender-limbed woman, whose childhood has been swallowed up by youth, some unprecedented artifice of graceful movement (*bhaṅgī*) has been adopted—a movement as full of the passion of the bodiless god (*Anaṅga*) as love itself—by means of which the Lord whose weapon is play (*vilāsāyudha*) triumphs in the sovereignty of the three worlds with effortless prowess, having abandoned his vast arsenal. By this statement, the name of Kāma as "the one whose weapon is play" is indeed justified; for when the desire to conquer and attain lordship over the three worlds is accomplished through the mere grace of the slender-limbed woman, the arrows and other weapons of Kāma become useless.
But it was not as with Kālidāsa, where even while the words of the gods in the sky were still sounding, "O Lord, withdraw your wrath! Withdraw it!",
that fire born from the eye of the Householder reduced Madana to nothing but ashes.

In this context, while the agitation caused by the falling of the arrows of Smara (the God of Love) was being described as the Blessed Lord Trinetra (Śiva) looked on, the words "Restrain, O Lord, restrain your anger" uttered by the gods in the sky for the sake of pacifying that [passion]—just as those words were coursing through the air, that fire born from the eye of Bhava reduced Madana to a mere heap of ashes.
Thus, at the moment of destruction, it is indeed inappropriate to address Rudra by the name "Bhava" (the one who comes into existence). 38.
To demonstrate the propriety of benedictory words, he says:
"For one who has bestowed the full meaning of poetry and satisfied the wise, an appropriate blessing brings about prosperity, just as it does for a king. (39)
For a poem that completely surrenders itself and has satisfied the learned, an appropriate benediction brings about prosperity, just as it does for a king;
such is the case with our teacher Gaṅgaka.
May that indescribable grace of the deer-eyed ones— moist with love, trembling with the fervor of affection, and manifest in their eyes— bestow upon you a bliss beyond compare;
for upon seeing its intent, they cover their faces within the hollows of their quivers.
The five arrows of the conqueror of the world have had their activity cast aside.

Herein lies that certain incomparable play of the eyes of the fawn-eyed ones, moistened by extraordinary love and resting in boldness; may it grant you happiness—that play which, upon perceiving its intent, the five arrows of Kāma, the conqueror of the world, seem to hide their faces within the hollows of their quivers out of shame, as if their work were finished. When it is said, "May it grant you happiness," this word of benediction is entirely appropriate, for the amorous play of the beloved’s eyes is fit for the bestowing of bliss. Or as in my *Vātsyāyanasūtrasāra*:
May Kāma— who dwells at the corners of the eyes of the lotus-faced woman,
who has reduced the inhabitants of the three worlds to servitude, and who remains worthy of the longing of all people even though he was burnt by the enemy of Tripura— arise for your delight.
The excellence of which has become exceedingly beautiful, like that of collyrium.

In this context, when it is said, "May desire arise for your pleasure, whose luster increases even when burnt, like collyrium," it is appropriate that it should arise for pleasure, because desire consists essentially of pleasure (*prīti*).
It is not, however, as in the verse of Amaruka: "Bearing her dangling row of *ālola* curls disheveled, and her shimmering swinging earrings... [and so forth].
May the face of the slender-limbed woman— its makeup slightly blurred by the finest droplets of perspiration at the conclusion of love-making during the reversal of roles—
protect you for a long time; what need is there for deities such as Hari, Hara, or Skanda?

In this context, regarding the verse: "May that face of the slender maiden—which, upon the reversal of sexual union, has dangling earrings, which is slightly blurred by drops of perspiration, and whose tilaka-mark is smudged—protect you! What need is there for deities such as Hari, Hara, Skanda, and the rest?"—the expression "may it protect you" (*pātu tvām*) is inappropriate; rather, "may it gladden you" (*ānandayatu tvām*) would be appropriate.
In other elements of poetry, propriety should be inferred by oneself in this same manner.
Since their examples are infinite, they have not been displayed here; enough of this digression. (40)
Introduction to the Author:
There was one named Prakāśendra, a light [of wisdom] in the land of Kāśmīra, possessing the glory of the Lord of the Thirty Gods (Indra).
In his house, there existed a pure sacrificial session (*sattra*) that was uninterrupted and served as the foremost seat for the eldest [of the lineage]. (1)
He who, in the wonderful and variegated temple of Śrī-Svayaṃbhū, established a circle of Mothers fashioned from plaster,
and who was a donor of cattle, land, and black antelope skins, at that very time cast off his body right there.
His son, a disciple of all the wise, whose auspicious and other holy names were Vyāsa,
Kṣemendra— whose fame for inexhaustible poetry is undying— composed this *Navaucityavicāracarcā*.
When his friend Śrī Ratnasiṃha had departed for the city of Śiva, the illustrious Queen Vijayeśvarī composed this expansion of words for the sake of her son named Udayasiṃha. || 4 ||

This was indeed composed at the time of the illustrious King Anantarāja, whose sword served as a protective guard, whose conduct and learning were renowned throughout the three worlds, by whom all [his subjects] attained supreme exaltation through their profound submission, and whose fire of valor incessantly brings coolness to the quarters of the earth.
Thus ends the *Aucityavicāracarcā*, composed by Śrī Kṣemendra, whose other name was Vayasadāsa, the son of Śrī Prakāśendra.
